title: Introduction to Contemporary African American Society
description: Survey of the characteristics and problems of African Americans in contemporary society.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: What is race? What is ethnicity? What are the legacies of racially and ethnically based discrimination in America? Matters related to race, ethnicity, and racism have been debated since the formation of the United States. However, while most people have some familiarity with these concepts, there is surprisingly little agreement on how to define these terms and their relative importance in American society. The course is designed for students that have not yet taken a similar course. The course goes beyond the social commentary and public opinion that we often find in newspapers and on social media and focuses instead on social scientific theory and systematic observations. After completing the course, students will have an introductory understanding of the conceptual nuances and complexities of race, ethnicity, and racism in the United States. The reading for the course is mostly from a textbook but also includes selected readings.

input: Introduction to Contemporary African American Society

title: AfAm Urban History
description: In-depth treatment of a key theme in black historical studies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Across the twentieth century, African American life transformed from a predominantly rural to a profoundly urban one. But how did this transformation occur? How and why did African American life become associated with the American city? How did African Americans contribute to building urban America as we know it today? This course will explore these questions and center the important role African Americans have played in building the American city. From the foundations of Black life in nineteenth century cities to the Great Migration and the transformation of urban centers in the twentieth to the so-called "urban crisis  of the 1970s, African Americans have had a significant impact on American cities as well as being profoundly shaped by the urban experience. Paying close attention to themes of race and place, this course will examine the contributions of African Americans to the social life, culture, economies, and politics of American cities.

title: Women and Slavery in the United States
description: A social history of women and race-based legal slaveholding in colonial British North America and the United States, 1619-1865. Special attention will be paid to enslaved Black women and slaveholding white women; discuss why there is so little scholarship about enslaved Indigenous women. Wrestle with the following questions: How and why was race-based slavery established in the colonies that would become the United States of America? How and why did gender conventions affect enslavement and slaveholding? How did enslaved and slaveholding women experience bondage and slaveholding over time and space? What are the structural legacies of race-based slavery and gender?

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is a social history of women and slavery in colonial North America and the United States, 1619-1865, we will explore three major themes: the origins and development of the institution of race-based slavery, the varied experiences of enslavement and enslavers, and finally the social, political, and economic effects of race-based slaveholding in the American Republic. Special attention will be paid to enslaved women of African descent and slaveholding white women. We will wrestle with the following questions: How and why was race-based slavery established in the colonies and how did those practices manifest in early American Republic? How and why did gender conventions affect enslavement and slaveholding? How and why did the experiences of women change over time and space? Finally, we will explore the social and structural legacies of race-based slavery and gender.

title: Historiography, Theory and Methods in Visual Culture
description: Focuses on the knowledge, theories, and methods that are fundamental to the transdisciplinary discipline of Visual Cultures. Develops skills in critical reading, research, analysis, writing, and oral presentation.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This seminar is the core requirement for the Doctoral Minor and Graduate certificate in the study of visual cultures, a field in which analytic attention to gender, sexuality and race is integral. The seminar charts the formation and history of the dynamic, multi-stranded, and still changing field in its critical dialogue with cultural studies, critical race theory and Black study, feminist theory, queer theory, trans studies and theory, disability studies and crip theory and performance studies. It seeks to build a practice-based knowledge of the theories and methods important to the field's formation as well as those driving the field's future. You will develop a set of skills in critical reading, research, analysis, writing, and presentation (including visual presentation methods) that will be of use to you throughout graduate school and in your professional life beyond. Toward these goals, the course has three main dimensions. As your introduction to the Doctoral Minor and Graduate Certificate here, the course will take advantage of the programming of the Center for Visual Cultures to frame your encounter with the leading questions driving the field, assist in facilitating the formation of a network and intellectual community, and help point you toward the research resources here that may support your work. As your introduction to practices in the study of visual cultures, the course explores the controversies that drove the field's formation, its complex relations to various disciplines and the issues, challenges, and debates fueling the ongoing transformations of the field. The readings are necessarily selective and partial. Thus, you are encouraged to use the syllabus as a map leading you to deepen your knowledge through further study. As a practicum, the seminar also emphasizes the development of essential skills in critical reading and analysis, primary and secondary research methods, the writing of various kinds of professional prose, oral presentation, and oral response to questions that are vital to your success in graduate study and future viability in the field. In addition to weekly readings and discussion, work for the course will include the generation of burning questions as the catalysts of inquiry, examining and analyzing the visual, producing and delivering oral presentations, and writing work that corresponds to specific kinds of professional writing. As this course is designed to enhance your professional formation, you are strongly encouraged to navigate the course architecture of readings and assignments according to the needs and dictates of your own research and developing areas of specialization.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
Sample structure of topics (subject to adjustment): 

Week 1: Introductions

Week 2: Care Webs and Mutual Aid 

Week 3: What are the Forms of Work in the Study of Visual Cultures? 

Week 4: What is the Object? 

Week 5: How do we approach the image; what do images do? 

Week 6: What is the visual in visual cultures; what is visuality? 

Week 7: What is the culture in visual cultures? 

Week 8: What is the role of aesthetics? 

Week 9: What/who is the Subject?

Week 10: How do I/We look/feel?

Week 11: How might we think at the limits of the visible, the evidentiary and the archive? 

Week 12: New Research Directions in Visual Studies

Week 13: Mutual Aid Workshop

Week 14: Symposium 

Week 15: Roundtable Reflections and Feedback
instructorProvidedContent.format: The course relies heavily on discussion participation and building intellectual community. The course requirements are designed to build toward the final project. Even if the burning question that guides our class discussion on the day you facilitate is not the one at the center of your final project, it is implicit in the sequence that the elements of the course represent a choreography of steps that lead to the final project. Engaging directly with the readings and works viewed and analyzed and the ideas encountered in seminar, M.A. and Ph.D. students will write a final paper and M.F.A. students will either write a final paper or produce a creative final project accompanied by a framing statement. The final project begins with the exercise of formulating and presenting a burning question addressed to an aspect of the readings in one of the weeks. In one of the last two weeks of the semester, you will present an overview of the main elements of your final project. You will submit a proposal for your final project and will be expected to incorporate feedback in the development of your final project. You will receive handouts in class with specific instructions.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
How do you represent a diverse continent of a billion people and 54 countries in just a few rooms in a museum? Can you? And why would you want to?

In this course students will learn about the history of putting "Africa" on display both on the continent and abroad, especially in the former colonial powers of Europe and in the United States. Students will question why Europeans began displaying objects from across the world, and why this practice continues today. They will also learn about museums and art spaces across the African continent -- what does it mean to "Africanize" the very European idea of a museum? We will also move beyond the walls of the museum to learn about biennials, independent artist-run spaces, and even how cities themselves are turned into exhibition spaces. Finally, we will address present issues around decolonizing museums, and the restitution and repatriation of objects from former colonies.

title: Tales of Love & War
description: Introduction to a special topic in African literature, focused on a specific region or genre.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
The texts we will study arise from a creative will to bring a new community into being. They are fueled, at the same time, by a desire to undo the destructive legacy of racism and oppression bequeathed by colonial domination.  Since, in several instances, this desire led to a protracted armed struggle against the colonial order, these creative expressions are in a sense born out of violence and war. In some cases, the bloodshed, in the form of brutal and devastating civil wars, lasted well into the post-independence period. Thus, by the end of the millennium, the lofty dream of a free, equitable and more just society lay in shambles. Throughout it all, cultural and literary expressions endured as a mode of bearing witness to often unspeakable pain and destruction. In the words of a Mozambican novelist, they remain also as a stubborn reminder that despite the violence, people tenaciously maintained their will to re-invent themselves, to convert the days of blood and horror into the stuff of hope and tenderness, endeavoring to produce order where chaos had entrenched itself, life and beauty where death had spread its mantle of agony and sorrow.

Our cultural and geographic areas of focus will be broad, encompassing Angola, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, South Africa, Sudan, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe.

title: Technology and Development in Africa and Beyond
description: Surveys the past 20 years of digital technology and communications culture on the African continent, cross-referenced with discourse on technology experiences in other parts of the developing world, through the framework of development studies. Readings include case studies of micro-tech practices as well as political and social use of new media, and government and NGO-led tech interventions. Information Communication Technology for Development (ICT4D) is a key area of focus. Cross-discipline areas include communications and media studies, African, Latin American and International area studies, as well as the social anthropology of technology and science, and design. Think critically about technology use in the context of different tech cultures from around the world. Apply this perspective towards new media solutions to social problems.

title: Global Health: Economics, Natural Systems, and Policy
description: Sustaining global health and well-being depends critically on interactions between human and natural systems at multiple spatial and temporal scales.  Economics provides a useful paradigm for understanding these interactions and the pathways through which individual and societal decisions made in the face of scarce resources, and threats to the natural environment, generate health and well-being outcomes.  Provides students with an opportunity to use basic economic and social science reasoning to describe global heath challenges; understand the causes and consequences of health discrepancies; evaluate health and environmental policies; and appreciate the interconnectedness of planetary health and economic outcomes.

title: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in Latin American society and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Brazil has long inspired curiosity in intellectual and artistic outsiders: from Michel de Montaigne's inauguration of the modern essay ("Of Cannibals,  1580) to Claude Levi-Strauss' notorious "writing lessons  in Tristes Tropiques (1955) to Michel Foucault's emergent theories of power in the 1970s and into Global Black studies of the 21st century. This interdisciplinary graduate seminar analyzes how Brazil   the place as well as the idea; the former colony and nation-state, as well as its representations   generates theory. Encounters and clashes among strikingly different peoples and worldviews shape how intellectuals and artists, both foreign and national, understand Brazil. Its staggering heterogeneity -- from pre-conquest cosmologies and especially beginning with the profoundly unequal European-Indigenous-African contact zones in the 15th and 16th centuries   makes it a singular incubator to understand theory as an inquiry into how knowledge grapples with what is new, unfamiliar, or unthinkable to it, as a perpetual search for knowledge in modernity, in worlds of mixture, conflict, and difference. The frequent motif of Brazil as a puzzle to both foreigners and Brazilians alike is perhaps best captured in political theorist Francisco de Oliveira's (2003) memorable metaphor of the duckbilled platypus, a walking paradox: at once reptile, bird, mammal - all three or none of these. In this course, we will trace how a Brazil imagined   "in theory,  in our everyday language, means an untested hypothesis   is also a story about what theory is and does. We will read theoretical essays by Brazilian and international thinkers and analyze works of the visual and literary arts from Brazil as aesthetic theory. The course will be of special interest to students of postcolonial or decolonial thought and Latin American/Caribbean studies. No knowledge of Brazil or Latin America is required. Students with reading knowledge of Portuguese will be encouraged to read in the original language.

title: Agroecological Systems: Working Towards Sustainability
description: Explores in-depth agriculture systems as coupled ecological and social complexities. Examines the components of agricultural systems and analyzes how different ecological and social contexts influence and are influenced by the agricultural system. Explores and analyzes how management decisions (crop breeding, in-crop management, landscape-level, etc.) ramify to influence processes and outcomes at different levels of complexity (e.g., ecosystem, landscape, social well-being, human health, economic) and the socio-ecological tradeoffs that ensue. Develops skills to analyze how the design and implementation of integrated agricultural systems can contribute to solutions for pressing societal challenges such as climate change, biodiversity declines, unsustainable resource use and social inequality.

Apply theories from across the humanities to interpret plants and ecological themes in religious practices, works of art, literature, architecture, and gardens. Think critically about the similarities and differences between your own use and understanding of plants and those of larger global communities.

title: Indigenous Peoples and the Environment
description: Indigenous peoples often have very close relationships to ancestral homelands, species and natural resources. However, definitions of "indigenous" can be controversial and highly politicized. Diverse outlooks on identities, worldviews and environmental governance clarify the complex meanings of indigeneity in the US. Highlights American Indian perspectives, conservation practices, and policy environments through consideration of US and international case studies. American Indian experiences shed light on pressing issues of resource sustainability and sovereignty, and demonstrate linkages to global Indigenous environmental issues and strategies.

description: Develop an upper intermediate level of the Ojibwe writing system and examine the associated morphology and syntactical verb structures. Develop literacy and an understanding of the unique verb-based sentence structures, and utilize conversational skills currently being used among Ojibwe speakers. title: Archaeology and the Prehistoric World
description: Introduction to the ancient world from origins of human culture to the beginnings of written history as revealed by archaeological research at great sites and ruins around the globe. Archaeological analyses of important sites as case studies to illustrate concepts and techniques used by archaeologists in their efforts to understand the diversity of the human past.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is for non-majors who are interested in the distant human past the period of time for which there are few written records and most of our knowledge about ancient human behavior comes to us from archaeological research. We discuss many of the best-known archaeological sites in the world as well as major developments in human biological and social evolution, including hunting, the capacity for abstract thought, the origins of agriculture and cities, technological innovations, and concepts of identity in the past. This course is co-taught by professors who specialize in the archaeology of distinct world regions and will present current research in their areas of specialization through readings, lectures and select films. We enjoy teaching this course and we hope that you will enjoy taking it!

title: Principles of Archaeology
description: Introduction to the methods, historical development, and scientific principles of archaeology. Discover how archaeologists generate and interpret information about the human past. Introduces scientific inquiry and provides a foundation for pursuing advanced archaeological courses and field research.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This course introduces students to the historical development, scientific principles, and methods of archaeology. The course begins with an overview of the historical development of the discipline that provides a context for the evolving practice of archaeology today. Archaeology is the study of the human behavior from material remains and the traces of these remains. -- the trash left behind by people. Our central goal is to use these remains to build inferences about human behavior, social organization, economies, political structures, technologies, and more. Some of the work that archaeologists do is exciting and thrilling(!), some is fun(!), but some is painstaking and slow-paced. Through a combination of lecture, discussion, and laboratory activities, students discover how archaeologists generate and interpret information about the human past. The course familiarizes students with scientific inquiry, provides experience in making observations and building interpretations from those observations, introduced students to the inherent interdisciplinarity of archaeology, and provides a foundation for pursuing advanced archaeological courses and field research.

In this course, students will learn how archaeologists obtain data, how they analyze and evaluate data, and how they re-analyze data to reconstruct and interpret human behavior in the past. The course will also address why some explanations about the past are more acceptable to archaeologists than others. This course will challenge students to develop and apply their critical thinking skills to archaeological problems as they generate and evaluate competing hypotheses about human behavior and provide evidence to support their conclusions and inferences about past behavior.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course provides an overview of the archaeology and early history of East and Southeast Asia. It begins with the earliest inhabitants and societies of the regions. We will will take a tour through time, starting with the Ice Ages, moving through the Holocene, and landing in recent historic periods. Along the way we will examine major developments such as the advent of agriculture, emerging forms of urbanism, and the underpinnings of various civilizations. We will also consider how present-day communities and stakeholders view, preserve, and make use of the materials and sacred sites of the past. The course thus also covers how the interpretation of the past is related to modern-day issues of historical reconstruction, nationalism, and cultural heritage. Students will become familiar with the major archaeological sites, prehistories, and early histories of the regions. All majors are welcome and the course assumes no prior knowledge of archaeology.

title: Archaeology of Warfare and Human Nature
description: Introduction to the evidence, debates, and theories related to violence and warfare in the human past, and how related behaviors are linked to the evolution of our species and modern manifestations of war. Highlights archaeological methods that recognize past warfare practices. Using case studies from the Pleistocene to the present, explores variations of warfare from all over the world. Topics considered include 1) the highly variable nature of violence and warfare in different cultural settings; 2) the antiquity of warfare; 3) how violence has shaped human societies. Historical and cross-cultural ethnographic research will be juxtaposed against archaeological cases to provide contextualized and data-rich examinations. Learn to critically evaluate arguments, claims, and interpretations made about war, peace, and human nature.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course deals with the archaeological and anthropological study of violence, warfare, peacemaking, and their potential links with human nature. We will take a tour around the world, considering contexts from the Ice Ages to the 21st century, exploring the evidence for early and modern forms of war. Discussed are the relevant data, debates, and theories, and how related behaviors may be linked to the evolution of our species and our societies. This includes aspects of aggression seen elsewhere in nature. Students will become familiar with how war has shaped, and has been transformed, by human cultures. Students will become better equipped to evaluate ongoing arguments and claims about war, peace, and human nature. All majors are welcome and the course assumes no prior knowledge of archaeology.

title: Music, Race, And Culture in Brazil
description: Focuses on music's significant role in the formation and maintenance of Brazilian national identity. Learn how a variety of Brazilian individuals, groups, and institutions have contributed to popular and scholarly debates about Brazilian culture, identity, and forms of belonging. These discussions will be anchored to important themes in Brazil's recent history, present, and imagined future, such as cultural cannibalism (antropofagia), and racial hybridity (mesticagem). Gain insight into how Brazilian artists and their audiences have debated race and racism through expressive means by analyzing a variety of anthropological and ethnomusicological texts about Brazilian popular music, literature, and its most famous annual ritual, Carnival.

title: Ancient Technology and Invention
description: The origins and development of early technologies. Impact of key prehistoric and pre-industrial inventions on the course of human evolution.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This course will focus on Experimental and Ethnoarchaeological approaches to the study of traditional technologies and material culture from all periods of human history and from all regions of the world. Technology and its role in human culture will be explored from many different perspectives including anthropological, art historical, scientific and ideological angles. The class will be structured as a seminar in which ancient and traditional technologies will be studied through readings, lectures, films and discussion, as well as the actual manufacture and examination of a wide range of artifacts. The course will include hands-on experimental components, including the production and manipulation tools and objects made from fiber, ceramics, glazes, antler, bone, shell, wood, copper/bronze and iron/steel. Using tools and samples provided to each student, class exercises during the first part of the course produce tools and objects that will be documented and analyzed in later parts of the course in order for students to learn how archaeologists study technologies. We will explore technologies involving stone and shell bead manufacture and pyrotechnology. Ceramic studies will include the preparation of clays and the study of clay properties as well as firing the pottery in a traditional outdoor kiln. We will also examine faience/glass making and finally metallurgy and students will be able to fire faience and cast brass or bronze objects using lost wax technique. By the end of the course students will have a basic understanding of major traditional technologies, the types of raw materials needed for manufacture and the waste fragments remaining from production. 
Each student will be required to complete hands-on laboratory exercises, oral presentations and written reports, as well as a final project incorporating some form of ancient or traditional technology. This course is set up to fulfill Comp B requirements and it is important that you hand in all assignments and take time to discuss any issues regarding writing and paper organization with me during my office hours. The procedures and results of your final project will be written up as a comprehensive research paper (details presented below) and presented to the class in person at the end of the course as a 15 minute PowerPoint presentation.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
After a brief introduction to the major themes and issues to be addressed in the course, we will begin with the study of fiber production followed by the production of stone tools and lithic raw materials and their various modifications. As we begin working on lithics we will also start exploring adhesives used in hafting, and then move to clays and ceramics, as well as pyrotechnology. We will also cover the techniques of recording, illustrating and photographing archaeological artifacts, such as lithics, pottery other objects in preparation for your future projects. Students will be provided in class with course supplies that are organized into weekly activities related to fibers, lithics, ceramics and metallurgy. Some of the items in the supply kit (10x hand lens, bronze drills etc) will need to be returned at the end of the course, but the raw materials and objects produced will not need to be returned. The subsequent sessions will focus on glazed ceramics and metals, including the production of lost wax models and bronze casting using traditional techniques. The pottery and clay objects will be fired in an updraft kiln at the outdoor experimental archaeology laboratory near Picnic Point during the summer if the campus is open for this type of activity. The faience objects will be fired in a muffle furnace in the Experimental Archaeology Lab and the lost wax models will be cast in an outdoor facility depending on what the University allows at that time. Actual manufacture of objects will take place during each course period and each student will be responsible for supplying their own leather work gloves, work clothing, pencils (3H and 5H), a centimeter ruler and eraser. Protective eyeglasses, a 10X hand lens and necessary supplies and raw materials will be provided.  

Each student will prepare a research paper relating to some aspect of ancient or traditional technology in the broadest sense; i.e. any activity that involves some variety of raw materials that has the potential of being preserved in the archaeological record. The research topic will require extensive online library research and may involve analyses of virtual archaeological collections and/or include the actual replication of specific objects or technologies. Each student will decide what they want to focus on and if special raw materials are needed they should consult with the instructor to determine where these would be available. Most raw materials are available from our experimental lab and other materials can be ordered for a specific study. The experimental manufacture of objects can take place in the available Anthro labs (Rm 5114 or 5124 or outdoor lab on Picnic Point) or other locations available to individual students. The instructor and TA will be available for in person and virtual consultation during the production process.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
"Archaeology of Mesoamerican Landscapes and Environments"
Undergraduate and graduate students are welcome! This course satisfies the capstone seminar requirement for the anthropology major and archaeology certificate. Feel free to contact Prof. Clayton at <sclayton@wisc.edu> with any questions you have about the class or for permission to enroll if you are not a declared major.

In this course we examine the ways in which people in Mesoamerica (Mexico and Central America) have modified, impacted, and experienced environments through time. We approach this subject primarily through an archaeological lens, but we also consider historical and ethnographic information to reconstruct human-environmental interaction. Through reading, discussion, and independent research, we will investigate the dynamic relationship between people and the cultural and natural landscapes that they inhabit, as well as social responses to climate change and shifting environmental conditions. We will examine these topics as they relate to Maya, Teotihuacan, and Aztec societies.
instructorProvidedContent.format: This is a student-centered, reading and writing-intensive seminar; no exams are given. This is not a lecture course, but a small-group workshop in which we learn about archaeological research concerning human-environmental interaction in Mesoamerica. Students are expected to read assigned literature, lead and contribute to discussions, conduct independent research, and present their work to the class. Critical thinking, verbalizing ideas, and active listening are central to this course.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This special topics course focuses on diasporic Latin American populations in North America and elsewhere. We will also, however, examine diasporic populations within Latin America, comparing migratory, cultural, and economic flows within and beyond Latin America. In so doing, we will consider contemporary and historical constructions of 'Latin America' as a region and interrogate 'Latin American' as an identity. Through our anthropologically grounded discussion of Latin American diasporas and diasporas in Latin America, we will consider themes like migration, (de)colonization, imperialism, capitalism, racialization, and ethnicization. Ethnographic as well as humanistic texts and other media will structure our conversations.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
The class will be structured as a seminar in which advanced archaeology, biological and cultural anthropology graduate students will be able to develop and refine their knowledge of basic practices and procedures in archaeology with a focus on research methods related to the Ph D Dissertation research and post-research dissertation writing process. This includes formulating an appropriate research design, developing innovative data analyses and interpretive models, refining writing skills, developing engaging presentation and teaching skills.
This course is intended to help students develop and formulate innovative and well organized dissertation research proposals as well as develop skills in submitting research proposals, organizing conferences, preparing CV and other documents needed for a successful career in archaeology, biological or cultural anthropology. One of the main objectives of this course is to provide a setting in which Anthropology graduate students, can learn to critically and constructively assess archaeological and anthropological research on ancient and heritage communities/cultures, technology, experimental archaeology, and ethnoarchaeology in the field of their choice. 
The final course assignment will be in the form of a dissertation proposal (or publishable article) with appropriate illustrations, figures, graphs, appendices, bibliography, etc.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
This course will require a significant amount of reading and library research, laboratory time and artifact analysis, as well as writing and presentation. The credit standard for this course is met by an expectation of a total of 135 hours of student engagement with the courses learning activities (at least 45 hours per credit), which include regularly scheduled instructor: student meeting times, reading, writing, problem sets, lab work, and other student work as described in the syllabus.
There will be weekly assignments and student presentations on each major topic such as: Current Archaeological and Anthropological Research Trends, Research Design and Implementation, NSF Dissertation Grant requirements, University and Federal Compliance policies, Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval process, CV preparation, Conference Presentations, Book Reviews,

title: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in Latin American society and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Brazil has long inspired curiosity in intellectual and artistic outsiders: from Michel de Montaigne's inauguration of the modern essay ("Of Cannibals,  1580) to Claude Levi-Strauss' notorious "writing lessons  in Tristes Tropiques (1955) to Michel Foucault's emergent theories of power in the 1970s and into Global Black studies of the 21st century. This interdisciplinary graduate seminar analyzes how Brazil   the place as well as the idea; the former colony and nation-state, as well as its representations   generates theory. Encounters and clashes among strikingly different peoples and worldviews shape how intellectuals and artists, both foreign and national, understand Brazil. Its staggering heterogeneity -- from pre-conquest cosmologies and especially beginning with the profoundly unequal European-Indigenous-African contact zones in the 15th and 16th centuries   makes it a singular incubator to understand theory as an inquiry into how knowledge grapples with what is new, unfamiliar, or unthinkable to it, as a perpetual search for knowledge in modernity, in worlds of mixture, conflict, and difference. The frequent motif of Brazil as a puzzle to both foreigners and Brazilians alike is perhaps best captured in political theorist Francisco de Oliveira's (2003) memorable metaphor of the duckbilled platypus, a walking paradox: at once reptile, bird, mammal - all three or none of these. In this course, we will trace how a Brazil imagined   "in theory,  in our everyday language, means an untested hypothesis   is also a story about what theory is and does. We will read theoretical essays by Brazilian and international thinkers and analyze works of the visual and literary arts from Brazil as aesthetic theory. The course will be of special interest to students of postcolonial or decolonial thought and Latin American/Caribbean studies. No knowledge of Brazil or Latin America is required. Students with reading knowledge of Portuguese will be encouraged to read in the original language.

input: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area

title: Principles of Biotechnology
description: Principles and techniques pertaining to biotechnology and its applications to our society. Survey of classical and emerging techniques.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Ethics, Safety, and Regulatory Environments in Biotechnology
description: Ethical and safety concerns in development, production, funding, and application of biotechnology. Analysis of socioeconomic impacts. Understanding the importance of data integrity. Overview of risk assessment and management in a regulatory environment designed to ensure safety of workers, study subjects, and patients, and protect intellectual property, data, and the environment.

input: Ethics, Safety, and Regulatory Environments in Biotechnology

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Professional and Technical Communication in Biotechnology
description: Application and analysis of professional scientific communication, both written and oral. Focuses on designing documents that convey complex, data-rich technical and scientific content to audiences with diverse information needs using a variety of professional genres, including reports, proposals, presentations, and documentation.

input: Professional and Technical Communication in Biotechnology

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Techniques in Biotechnology
description: Application of biological and chemical methods to modern biotechnological product development. Overview of analysis techniques used to characterize products and evaluate quality and safety. Exploration of technological pipeline from conception to market, including proof-of-concept assessment, pre-clinical trials, clinical trials, and post-production testing.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

enrollmentPrerequisites: Declared in MS Applied Biotechnology or Capstone Certificate in Applied Bioinformatics
title: Experimental Design and Analysis in Biotechnology
description: Principles of descriptive and inferential statistics with applications in biotechnology including experimental design, quantitative data analysis, and bioinformatic evaluation of complex molecular and biological data sets.

input: Experimental Design and Analysis in Biotechnology

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Leadership in Organizations
description: Focuses on strategies and tools that managers use to maximize employee contribution and create organizational excellence. Basic business and leadership principles. Best practices to overcome biases that inhibit organizations and teams from communicating effectively. Examples will come from diverse biotechnology fields, including pharmaceutics, agriculture, and biotechnology services.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

enrollmentPrerequisites: Declared in MS Applied Biotechnology or Capstone Certificate in Applied Bioinformatics
title: Python for Bioinformatics
description: Introduce diverse strategies for computational analysis of macromolecular data using Python including sequence alignment, genome annotation, data retrieval from databases, phylogenetic analysis, and molecular evolution. Experiential learning is emphasized; confidence in practical skills is developed through persistent application of course content to projects focused on current problems in bioinformatic research.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Quality Control and Validation
description: Focuses on the importance of quality control and validation in biotechnology product design, development, and manufacturing. Explores quality systems and documentation, global quality standards, and methods for assessing validation including installation, operational, and performance qualifications. Overviews biomanufacturing processes, automation, and cGLP/cGMP practices necessary to meet quality standards.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Regulatory Practice and Compliance
description: Identifies and examines the key regulatory agencies and practices that govern the highly regulated and diverse biotechnology industry, both domestically and internationally. Highlights current and emerging FDA and ICH regulations and guidance documents to successfully navigate meeting with the agencies and to submit required documentation for successful product development.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Biotechnology Marketing and Entrepreneurship
description: Examines marketing case studies in diverse areas of biotechnology. Addresses marketing fundamentals and strategies, communicating value proposition strategy, ethical and regulatory concerns, startup strategies, pharmaceutical marketing, b2b marketing, salesforce development, branding, and promotion. Culminates with the creation of a marketing plan/analysis.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Assessing Innovation in Biotechnology
description: A survey of biotechnology assessments in areas such as regenerative medicine, agricultural biotechnology, and bioremediation. Course links disciplines with the critical evaluative role played by scientific discovery, market valuation, intellectual property, freedom-to-operate (FTO), and licensing strategy by assessing the role each played in the commercialization of a specific technology.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Product Development
description: Explores strategies in evaluating and implementing new technologies or products in the context of different bioindustries. Identifies considerations in product valuation, feasibility of production, scalability, and supply chain management. Models the process of business growth and innovation through integration of emerging technologies.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Application of Bioinformatics
description: Exploration and application of existing bioinformatic tools. Implementation of pre-coded solutions to data acquisition, wrangling, analysis, visualization, and structural modeling problems. Complete a project that generates a multi-system workflow to solve bioinformatic problems.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Pre-Capstone
description: Prepares the student for applied self-directed capstone experience. Addressing problem identification, research, and project formulation. Culminates in an oral and written proposal with project schedule.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Capstone
description: Complete a project (report, business plan, program, etc.) in an area of quality assurance and compliance, business and management, and/or research and development. Culminating in a substantive body of work, executive summary, and reflection. Networking and communication in a professional capacity is expected.

title: 3D Digital Studio I
description: Introduction to three-dimensional modeling in the computer, in particular the use of 3D digital models for the creation of images and objects.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This class is the first in a two class series which will introduce you to 3D digital modeling and animation software as a tool for making art. In this class we will look at modeling materials and lighting. The class will also explore aesthetic and design issues that are relevant to these techniques. Lectures will introduce you to contemporary practice in the field. We will look at the work of a variety of artists and designers who use advanced 3D digital modeling in one way or another. 
As well as teaching a variety of digital tools this class will explore their creative potential beyond the "traditional  fields of Computer Generated Imagery, by which I mean game design, VFX, and narrative animation. Much of the work we will be looking at exists outside the commercial arena, which means that is not necessarily designed to tell a straightforward story or to sell a product.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
In class we will be working primarily with Autodesk Maya. You will also need an image editing program like Adobe Photoshop or a freeware alternative like GIMP. Software that we will be looking at but that will NOT BE REQUIRED for the class will include Autodesk Mudbox and Adobe Substance 3D Painter.
By completing this class students will learn the following

o	Be able to create polygonal models using a variety of techniques.
o	Understand shaders including the ability to create and use complex shader networks using procedural and image based textures.
o	Understand texture projection techniques as well the editing of mesh UVs to control textures in your shaders.
o	Understand camera setup and lighting including the ability to create and use the full range of lights.
o	Understand rendering including the ability to render photo-real and non-photo-real images using a number of different renderers.
o	Understand contemporary practice in the field, including the use of 3D digital technology in fine art, design and entertainment.
o	Graduate students will be able to incorporate techniques and information covered by the class into their own research.

title: The End of the World
description: Do you feel anxious? Are thoughts of an impending apocalypse - whether by plague, war, climate disaster, or sentient robots - bringing you down?  We are not the first to face the end of the world. Explore how artists have grappled with the world's end through case studies across space and time. Why are we drawn to apocalyptic narratives? What can they tell us about humanity's shared fears and hopes? How does art anticipate and rebuild from cataclysm?  Peer into the abyss to contemplate the end of the world as we know it. Emerge with an appreciation for the enduring resilience of the human condition.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Do you feel anxious? Are thoughts of an impending apocalypse -- whether by plague, war, climate disaster, or sentient robots -- bringing you down? We are not the first to face the end of the world. Explore how humanity has grappled with the world's end across space and time. Anchoring our analysis in the history of art, we will also explore dystopian imaginings in television, film, video games, and literature. Why are we drawn to apocalyptic narratives? What can they tell us about humanity's shared fears and hopes? How does art anticipate and rebuild from cataclysm? This class is about the end of the world. But it is also about hope and the enduring resilience of the human spirit.

title: History of Western Art II: From Renaissance to Contemporary
description: Examine the arts and culture of Europe and North America from the Renaissance through the present. Explore important fine art, architecture, decorative arts, and photographic masterpieces by artists like Leonardo da Vinci, Rembrandt van Rijn, Claude Monet, Paul Cezanne, Pablo Picasso, Frida Kahlo, and Frank Lloyd Wright. Learn how works of art were valued from the moment of their making, fought over by different nations, bought, sold, stolen, or ignored for centuries and revived only recently for study through the political, historical, social and cultural contexts of their making. Critically examine the concept of artistic genius; the influence of colonialism and imperialism on artistic production and consumption; the role of the patron and the art market in art's production and circulation; the relationship of fine art and popular culture; and the idea of globalization as it relates to "western" artistic traditions. Develop skills in visual analysis to understand artistic production.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Come explore the many reasons that art has been produced and the vast array of forms it has taken in Europe and what is now called the United States during the past 500 years. Examining famous and iconic artworks by the likes of Michelangelo, Vermeer, Van Gogh, and Warhol, the class will consider the relationship between artists and their cultures-- clothing, personal relationships, medicine, religious or social beliefs, scientific discoveries, or desires and taboos. Lectures will explore what motivated, inspired, awed, and frightened artists in different places and at points in time. We will learn skills to enable us to intelligently describe and interpret works of painting, sculpture, architecture, photography and decorative arts. We will also take stock of the ways in which what we call "art" operates in a context of power - how it has been used to build up those in power and marginalize others.

title: The Modernist Revolution
description: Overview of the emergence and development of modernism in the visual arts between approximately 1880 and 1970, begining with the origins of modernist visual art in the late 19th century, then moving on to the proliferation of avant-garde movements in the first half of the 20th century before concluding with the crisis and collapse of modernism in the post-World War II period. Movements covered include Cubism, Futurism, Dadaism, Surrealism, and Abstract Expressionism. Major topics: the breakdown of traditional pre-modernist artistic styles and genres; invention of radical new techniques such as abstraction and collage; impacts of the political, social, and technological upheavals of the modern era; relations between modernist art, racialization, and colonialism; the transition between modernism and contemporary (or post-modernist) art.

title: Myths, Loves, and Lives in Greek Vases
description: Explore the world of the ancient Greeks through their painted pottery. Greek pottery offers a uniquely rich imagery of mythology, athletics, domestic scenes, fabulous monsters, drinking parties, and other aspects of Greek life and imagination. They were used by ordinary people, and their use offers insights into their everyday lives and concerns, and a counterbalance to the elite accounts preserved in literature and poetry. Consider the long history of Greek vases from about 800 BC until about 350 BC, and focus on themes such as relationships with the East, myth and epic poetry, narrative, and everyday subjects such as women's lives, death and the afterlife, and the symposium. Make use of the excellent collection of Greek vases in the Chazen Museum, and write research papers using that collection.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
AH 303.  Global India: Cross-Cultural Architectural Connections

This lecture course concentrates on India and South Asia's global architectural histories from the ancient to the modern periods.  While focusing predominantly on architectural sites in India, it examines architecture at multiple sites across the globe which share connected histories with South Asia.

This course examines India and South Asia's global architectural histories not only through comparison but, in the words of historian Sanjay Subrahmanyam, "by seeking out the at times fragile threads that connected  India to "the globe.   The sites for this architectural history are both within and beyond South Asia.  This course captures the mobility of populations, traders, conquerors, missionaries, pilgrims, tourists, colonists, architects, artists, scholars, religion, merchandise, art, architecture, ideas and so on as well as parallel developments taking place across the globe.  In doing so, we show that South Asia's global architectural histories escape the nation state and are themselves the complex products of varied histories of cultural encounters.  No prior knowledge of India is necessary.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
From granary-inspired Shinto shrines to Olympic stadiums rendered in concrete and steel, the history of Japanese architecture encompasses a diverse tradition of building. This course explores the history of Japanese architecture from prehistoric to modern times. The types of buildings we will study include Shinto shrines, Buddhist temples, multi-story pagodas, fortified castles, elite and commoner residential structures, and teahouses. In the course, students will learn about the principles of timber frame engineering, native versus adopted architectural idioms, the relationship between architecture and the environment, and the role of architecture and architectural space in engendering particular contexts of function, use, and meaning.

Course Learning Outcomes
 - Acquire understanding of the major technological, stylistic, historical, religious, social, and functional developments that have shaped the history of Japanese architecture from ancient times to the twentieth century.
 - Learn to analyze a structure by considering how it was built and why it looks the way it does.
 - Cultivate the skills of visual literacy and critical thinking.
 - Practice persuasive writing and effective communication.

Requisites
Sophomore standing

title: Romanesque and Gothic Art and Architecture
description: Art and architecture of Western Europe, ca. 1000 to ca. 1350. Particular emphasis on the relaionship of the arts to theology, ritual, concepts of the body, rulership and courtliness.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course explores art and architecture as the agents and reflections of significant social and religious change, globalization and trade, scientific and technological change that shaped an emergent European identity from the second half of the eleventh century to the beginning of the fifteenth century.  Focusing principally on France, Northern Spain and Italy, we will consider such topics as sculpture in relation to the senses and religious experience, the architecture of pilgrimage, monsters, gender, and alterity, portraiture and the commemoration of the dead, female mysticism and devotional images, mappaemundi and cartography, technological innovation and visionary experience in the architecture of Gothic cathedrals,  the world of nature in medieval scientific manuscripts, and the macabre arts of late medieval funerary culture.  In addition, particular emphasis will be placed on the interaction of Western Europe with the cultures of the Eastern Mediterranean through trade, pilgrimage, conquest and crusade.

title: 19th Century Painting in Europe
description: History of European painting from 1800 to 1900.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
AH350 "19th-Century Painting in Europe, or "Rebels and Revolution: European Painting in the 1800s"

This survey course situates the important artists and artworks of the period in their cultural and historical contexts. Topics include French, British, and German art movements, focusing on Romanticism, Pre-Raphaelitism, Realism, Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, and photography, with a thematic focus on issues of gender, race, and the important political and philosophical questions of the era.

Explore the century that gave us the world as we know it now: light-bulbs, steam engines, reproductive technologies, the mass media, phonographs, telegraphs, telephones, factories, the middle class, globalization, condoms, antisepsis, even computers! How did artists respond to and participate in an era of rapid change not unlike our own? A time of paradigm shifts in Western ways of understanding the world, the nineteenth century in Europe saw the emergence of new ideas like the equality of all humans preached by the French Revolution, the concept of childhood, Freudian psychoanalysis, Marxism,  animal rights, and Darwinian evolutionary theory, among other new ideas.  The nineteenth-century legacy also includes darker aspects of modernity related to its privileging of white middle-class men, such as colonialism and racial and sexual inequalities.

title: Chinese Textiles and Paper
description: In-depth examination of special topics related to Asian art, including South Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This course is being developed in conjunction with an exhibition on the Chinese Hell, scheduled to open in 2027. The Chinese concept of hell is not a singular or unified idea, but rather a complex system of afterlife realms involving judgment, punishment, and, at times, redemption. During the late imperial period, scenes depicting underground courts and punishments were often staged as part of opera performances during the Festival of Feeding Hungry Ghosts.
The exhibition features a rare collection of Chinese hell imagery and artifacts from the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago, gathered by anthropologist Berthold Laufer (1874--1934) in China during the early 20th century. In addition, it includes stage settings, costumes, and ephemeral sculptures primarily made from fabric and papier-m ch . These objects once served as didactic tools used to convey Buddhist, Daoist, and Confucian moral principles on Chinese stages and in temple courtyards. They were integral to the annual ritual calendar of local communities.
Drawing on collections from the Field Museum and the Helen Louise Allen Textile Collection on campus, students in this course will engage with research methods in the visual and material history of Chinese opera and develop ideation techniques to shape curatorial concepts. The course offers both conceptual frameworks and practical tools for translating these ideas into a fully realized exhibition design within a physical gallery space.

title: Contemporary Queer Art and Visual Culture
description: Queer art and visual culture are defined not only through their subject matter but also by the methods through which they appropriate and subvert conventional visual practices. Such tactics may include a work's means of production, its formal properties, and the conditions of its reception. The political imperatives of a queer or queered position, linked to the intersections of race, class, sex and gender will shape thematic investigations of practices related to activism, documentation, abstraction, mining the archive, craft, camp, and drag, among others. Case studies will be drawn from film, performance, comics, video games, and fine art. Projects will engage text- and studio-based research in an interdisciplinary push to integrate theory and practice. No prior art or design experience required. Not open to students with credit for GEN&WS 412 prior to Fall 2026.

title: The Art of Our Time
description: Outline of major developments in global visual art from the 1960s to the present, with an emphasis on influential recent theorizations of contemporary art that have been developed by critics, art historians, and artists themselves. Topics include: the globalization of the art world, re-definitions of art after modernism, politics of contemporary art, issues of identity (race, gender, sexuality), technology and new media, the art market, and theoretical approaches to contemporary art.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Art is one of the basic ways in which humans reflect upon themselves and their experiences. But the landscape of contemporary art can often seem daunting. Even apart from the prevalence of obscure jargon and gatekeeping in the art world, the field of recent artistic production strikes many outsiders and some experts, too as a set of random trends lacking the coherence of great artistic styles of the past. Others claim that, rather than being too inaccessible, contemporary art has on the contrary become mere entertainment (or a mere luxury commodity), declining from the intellectual rigor of the earlier avant-garde. Still others complain that recent art has become excessively politicized, prizing ideological purity over aesthetic achievement.

The point of this course is to argue that we should nonetheless take contemporary art seriously some of it, anyway. Since the collapse of modernism (generally dated to the 1960s), artists have had to confront a situation in which it appears that anything can be art: random scatters of trash on the floor; readymade objects bought off the shelf; short conceptual statements without any physical manifestation at all. From this vastly expanded range of possibilities, certain artists have developed compelling, strange, and sometimes disturbing practices that raise important questions about contemporary existence.

We will try to understand these practices through a series of deep dives. There happen to be fifteen weeks in the UW Madison fall semester. Our first and last weeks will consist of an overall introduction and conclusion to the course, respectively. In October there will also be a week to review for and then take your midterm exam. In November, Thanksgiving week will have a single meeting for free discussion and reflection on topics that have emerged in the course so far. That leaves eleven weeks of pure instruction. Each of these eleven weeks will be dedicated to a single artist (all living with exception of Mike Kelley, whose death came before its time). This selection of artists is not meant to be exhaustive or even representative of the contemporary art scene. I have, instead, chosen artists about whom I try think deeply and whose work, I feel, rewards careful attention. The organization of the class is therefore neither chronological nor exactly thematic. Considering these individual artists will nonetheless open perspectives on broader artistic tendencies over the past fifty years or so, thus addressing the issues flagged in the course guide description.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
AH 500. INDIA LOOKS EAST: VISUAL & SPATIAL CULTURES OF ASIA

With a focus on modern South Asia, this seminar will also look to the East of India to explore the visual and spatial cultures of Southeast and East Asia.  For millennia, these different regions have shared a connected history.  However, since European colonial rule, our attention has often turned to the West.  This seminar brings South Asia into conversation with Southeast and East Asia, and sometimes to other parts of the world.  We will study selected aspects of the religious, visual, and material cultures, as well as the architecture and urbanism of these regions.  In doing so, we will begin to explore the rich diversity of the visual and spatial cultures of South, Southeast and East Asia.

description: Advanced  topics in Ancient Art History taught in a seminar-style format.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Art and Loot

This seminar will examine the complex relationships among art, context, collecting, cultural property and heritage, and a host of related questions. Since antiquity, people have gathered and displaced works of art, particularly those of other cultures, in acts of conquest, imperialism, and similar processes. On the one hand, great works of art from many different cultures can now be seen side by side in museums around the world, inviting and promoting greater cultural understanding and appreciation. On the other hand, the illicit antiquities market today ranks behind only arms and drugs as the highest-grossing criminal trade, and it has led to the wholesale destruction of ancient sites in the search for loot.

We will organize the semester around a series of case studies, to try to understand the phenomena, follow its development through history, and consider current reactions, practices, and legislation.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course will explore the world of the ancient Greeks through their painted pottery. Greek pottery offers a uniquely rich imagery of mythology, athletics, domestic scenes, fabulous monsters, drinking parties, and other aspects of Greek life and imagination. They were used by ordinary people, and their use offers insights into their everyday lives and concerns, and a counterbalance to the elite accounts preserved in literature and poetry. The course will consider the long history of Greek vases from about 800 BC until about 350 BC, and focus on themes such as relationships with the East, myth and epic poetry, narrative, and everyday subjects such as women's lives, death and the afterlife, and the symposium.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
TOPIC: Illuminating the Word: Image and Story, Ritual and Prayer in Premodern Manuscript Books (Exhibition course)
One of the most significant technological innovations in late antiquity was the replacement of the papyrus rotulus (roll) by the parchment codex or manuscript (hand-written book) as principal vehicle for the dissemination of the written word. Habits of reading and organizing knowledge were transformed in ways comparable to the digital revolution in our own time. Script was transformed into art by the introduction of decorated or inhabited letters, and complex image programs offered visual interpretations of the texts they accompanied. Focusing on global manuscript culture of distinct religious traditions, this course will prepare a physical exhibition for UW Special Collections, showcasing premodern books and single leaves from campus collections and some private collections. The purpose of this class is threefold: 1) to explore the history of the premodern book within multiple cultural and religious traditions, examining the interpretive role of images and script 2) to consider the afterlife of the premodern book in both early printed books and modern recreations and facsimiles 3) to learn the craft of preparing an exhibition of physical objects, including issues of display, accessible label copy, publicity and public programming.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Required of all first-semester graduate students of art history and recommended to all art-history-curious grads, this seminar focuses on both pragmatic skills and on introducing you to the wide variety of approaches in the field of art history.  We will review the historiography of the field, examining how the scope of "art history" has changed over time, particularly as scholars have expanded their domain of study beyond western objects and media and incorporated critical theory as well as ideas/methods from other disciplines. In exposing yourself to the vast arena that art historical practice now encompasses, and by critically assessing the range of tools available, you can begin to develop a critical self-consciousness about your own approaches and situate them relative to the discipline as a whole. We focus in particular on developing the various skills necessary for art historical careers (e.g., academic, curatorial, information-science or art-market-related)

The aims of this course are three-fold:  first, to acquaint you with scholarly and visual resources; second, to explore the changing approaches to the practice of art history, from its origins through the present; and third, to develop essential skills in critical reading, research, writing, and oral presentation that are necessary to succeed in graduate study and as a professional in the field.  

REQUIREMENTS:
Weekly Reading Assignments  
Discussion Participation
Facilitating Discussion
Writing Assignments: Book Review, Application of Method, Conference Paper (Paper Proposal, Annotated Bibliography, Presentation, Final Paper)

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
AH707"19th-Century Painting in Europe, or "Rebels and Revolution: European Painting in the 1800s"

This is the graduate number for AH350. This course situates the important artists and artworks of the period in their cultural and historical contexts. Topics include French, British, and German art movements, focusing on Romanticism, Pre-Raphaelitism, Realism, Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, and photography, with a thematic focus on issues of gender, race, and the important political and philosophical questions of the era.

Explore the century that gave us the world as we know it now: light-bulbs, steam engines, reproductive technologies, the mass media, phonographs, telegraphs, telephones, factories, the middle class, globalization, condoms, antisepsis, even computers! How did artists respond to and participate in an era of rapid change not unlike our own? A time of paradigm shifts in Western ways of understanding the world, the nineteenth century in Europe saw the emergence of new ideas like the equality of all humans preached by the French Revolution, the concept of childhood, Freudian psychoanalysis, Marxism,  animal rights, and Darwinian evolutionary theory, among other new ideas.  The nineteenth-century legacy also includes darker aspects of modernity related to its privileging of white middle-class men, such as colonialism and racial and sexual inequalities.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course explores art and architecture as the agents and reflections of significant social and religious change, globalization and trade, scientific and technological change that shaped an emergent European identity from the second half of the eleventh century to the beginning of the fifteenth century.  Focusing principally on France, Northern Spain and Italy, we will consider such topics as sculpture in relation to the senses and religious experience, the architecture of pilgrimage, monsters, gender, and alterity, portraiture and the commemoration of the dead, female mysticism and devotional images, mappaemundi and cartography, technological innovation and visionary experience in the architecture of Gothic cathedrals,  the world of nature in medieval scientific manuscripts, and the macabre arts of late medieval funerary culture.  In addition, particular emphasis will be placed on the interaction of Western Europe with the cultures of the Eastern Mediterranean through trade, pilgrimage, conquest and crusade.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
AH 303.  Global India: Cross-Cultural Architectural Connections

This lecture course concentrates on India and South Asia's global architectural histories from the ancient to the modern periods.  While focusing predominantly on architectural sites in India, it examines architecture at multiple sites across the globe which share connected histories with South Asia.

This course examines India and South Asia's global architectural histories not only through comparison but, in the words of historian Sanjay Subrahmanyam, "by seeking out the at times fragile threads that connected  India to "the globe.   The sites for this architectural history are both within and beyond South Asia.  This course captures the mobility of populations, traders, conquerors, missionaries, pilgrims, tourists, colonists, architects, artists, scholars, religion, merchandise, art, architecture, ideas and so on as well as parallel developments taking place across the globe.  In doing so, we show that South Asia's global architectural histories escape the nation state and are themselves the complex products of varied histories of cultural encounters.  No prior knowledge of India is necessary.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
AH 800.  INDIA LOOKS EAST: VISUAL AND SPATIAL CULTURES OF ASIA

With a focus on modern South Asia, this seminar will also look to the East of India to explore the visual and spatial cultures of Southeast and East Asia.  For millennia, these different regions have shared a connected history.  However, since European colonial rule, our attention has often turned to the West.  This seminar brings South Asia into conversation with Southeast and East Asia, and sometimes to other parts of the world.  We will study selected aspects of the religious, visual, and material cultures, as well as the architecture and urbanism of these regions.  In doing so, we will begin to explore the rich diversity of the visual and spatial cultures of South, Southeast and East Asia.

title: Historiography, Theory and Methods in Visual Culture
description: Focuses on the knowledge, theories, and methods that are fundamental to the transdisciplinary discipline of Visual Cultures. Develops skills in critical reading, research, analysis, writing, and oral presentation.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This seminar is the core requirement for the Doctoral Minor and Graduate certificate in the study of visual cultures, a field in which analytic attention to gender, sexuality and race is integral. The seminar charts the formation and history of the dynamic, multi-stranded, and still changing field in its critical dialogue with cultural studies, critical race theory and Black study, feminist theory, queer theory, trans studies and theory, disability studies and crip theory and performance studies. It seeks to build a practice-based knowledge of the theories and methods important to the field's formation as well as those driving the field's future. You will develop a set of skills in critical reading, research, analysis, writing, and presentation (including visual presentation methods) that will be of use to you throughout graduate school and in your professional life beyond. Toward these goals, the course has three main dimensions. As your introduction to the Doctoral Minor and Graduate Certificate here, the course will take advantage of the programming of the Center for Visual Cultures to frame your encounter with the leading questions driving the field, assist in facilitating the formation of a network and intellectual community, and help point you toward the research resources here that may support your work. As your introduction to practices in the study of visual cultures, the course explores the controversies that drove the field's formation, its complex relations to various disciplines and the issues, challenges, and debates fueling the ongoing transformations of the field. The readings are necessarily selective and partial. Thus, you are encouraged to use the syllabus as a map leading you to deepen your knowledge through further study. As a practicum, the seminar also emphasizes the development of essential skills in critical reading and analysis, primary and secondary research methods, the writing of various kinds of professional prose, oral presentation, and oral response to questions that are vital to your success in graduate study and future viability in the field. In addition to weekly readings and discussion, work for the course will include the generation of burning questions as the catalysts of inquiry, examining and analyzing the visual, producing and delivering oral presentations, and writing work that corresponds to specific kinds of professional writing. As this course is designed to enhance your professional formation, you are strongly encouraged to navigate the course architecture of readings and assignments according to the needs and dictates of your own research and developing areas of specialization.

Week 1: Introductions

instructorProvidedContent.format: The course relies heavily on discussion participation and building intellectual community. The course requirements are designed to build toward the final project. Even if the burning question that guides our class discussion on the day you facilitate is not the one at the center of your final project, it is implicit in the sequence that the elements of the course represent a choreography of steps that lead to the final project. Engaging directly with the readings and works viewed and analyzed and the ideas encountered in seminar, M.A. and Ph.D. students will write a final paper and M.F.A. students will either write a final paper or produce a creative final project accompanied by a framing statement. The final project begins with the exercise of formulating and presenting a burning question addressed to an aspect of the readings in one of the weeks. In one of the last two weeks of the semester, you will present an overview of the main elements of your final project. You will submit a proposal for your final project and will be expected to incorporate feedback in the development of your final project. You will receive handouts in class with specific instructions.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Art and Loot

This seminar will examine the complex relationships among art, context, collecting, cultural property and heritage, and a host of related questions. Since antiquity, people have gathered and displaced works of art, particularly those of other cultures, in acts of conquest, imperialism, and similar processes. On the one hand, great works of art from many different cultures can now be seen side by side in museums around the world, inviting and promoting greater cultural understanding and appreciation. On the other hand, the illicit antiquities market today ranks behind only arms and drugs as the highest-grossing criminal trade, and it has led to the wholesale destruction of ancient sites in the search for loot.

We will organize the semester around a series of case studies, to try to understand the phenomena, follow its development through history, and consider current reactions, practices, and legislation.
