title: Asian American Literary and Popular Culture: Race, Fantasy, Futures
description: Explores fantasy as a conduit of political meaning in Asian American fiction, graphic novels, anime, and art. Analyzes race as it circulates in visual mediums and literary texts. Engages issues such as stereotyping, caricature, and microaggressions; whitewashing, yellowface, and passing; race fetishism; cultural appropriation; multiracialism; kawaii or cute style; techno- orientalism and virtual Asians. Foregrounding fantasies of bodilessness, examine race as it is grafted onto nonhuman forms-objects, digital avatars, robots-at the borders of science and fiction. Examines how projections of the future reflect cultural anxieties about race, immigration, and Asian Americans.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How is fantasy a conduit of political meaning in Asian American fiction, graphic novels, drama, and popular culture? We will analyze race as it circulates in visual mediums, commodities, and literary texts, engaging interdisciplinary issues such as racial stereotyping, caricature, and microaggressions; whitewashing, yellowface, and passing; race fetishism and sexual objectification; cultural appropriation; kawaii or cute style; food as metaphor; and science fiction. The course examines race as it is grafted onto nonhuman forms--objects, digital avatars, animals. We will examine how projections of the future reflect cultural anxieties about race, immigration, globalization, and Asians Americans. How do these projections of an invented "Asia" fuel or mitigate anti-Asian bias?

title: Afro Asian Improv: From Hip Hop to Martial Arts Fusion
description: An Afro Asian perspective provides a lens through which intersections between Asian American and African American dance and martial arts are studied and practiced. Asian American and African American movement genres provide tools to explore dance fusion, choreography, and improvisation, to create dances informed by African American and Asian American legacies of struggle, innovation and transformation, while cognizant of historical forces of oppression and racism. Building connections through respectful communication with others are learned through dance practice, discussion and writing about concepts learned through readings, videos, and guest artist visits. Engagement with dance as a cultural vehicle for creative problem-solving and risk-taking occurs through guided class or smaller group activities.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Ever felt intimidated by the idea of learning a foreign language?
Try Indonesian the national language of a vibrant, multicultural nation. Discover its easy-to-learn language, free of complex conjugations and inflections, yet rich in expression. Indonesian stands out for its straightforward grammar and phonetic spelling, making it an ideal starting point for language learners. Join us for live, interactive sessions on Zoom, where you can participate in collaborative activities in real time from anywhere.

As the fourth most populous country globally, the largest Muslim-majority nation, the third-largest democracy, and the sixteenth-largest economy, Indonesia offers a wealth of cultural and economic significance to explore through its language. 
By the end of the first semester, you will be able to conduct basic communication with Indonesian speakers. The class will ensure that you have plenty of support and interactions with your teacher, classmates, and other native speakers while engaging in various fun and stimulating activities. Many scholarships, including study abroad opportunities, await when you pursue further study in the language!

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: I am so excited to teach this course early--it was originally scheduled for Spring 2027, which is why I'm late posting this information. This course will teach you basic classical Japanese grammar & the basics of reading cursive/ calligraphic script so that you start to decode the writing on woodblock prints. There are no required books for this course. I will recommend some references, websites, and apps in class.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
For the first six weeks, we'll focus on classical Japanese poems (Waka) from the Heian and early medieval periods because they are short but still full of useful grammar; if you're totally confused, you can start fresh with the next poem. These poems will teach you how to understand the older forms of verbs and adjectives that were used for a millennium, including in nonliterary texts like government documents and even a few cookbooks!

At the same time that we're learning the basic grammar, we'll also start learning the most common hentaigana (variant kana) and the kanji from which they derive. This will help you to start figuring out how to read manuscripts and block printed texts (including their furigana).

After the first six weeks, we will transition to longer texts from different genres and eras so that you get a sense of the range of uses of Classical Japanese. If you have subjects that you're interested in, please email me before the semester starts! I will be happy to work them into the syllabus.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Mix of lecture & discussion. Lots of in-class practice/problem-solving & bonus historical/literary content.

title: Democracy and Tyranny in Asia
description: Offers a comparative and interdisciplinary introduction to multiple cultures of Asia. Possible topics include but are not limited to: travelogues; the languages of Asia; food cultures of Asia.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This course offers an introduction to the politics of democracy and tyranny across Asia. Through systematic comparisons of the diverse experiences of Asian societies, the course traces moments of social and political change that often center on contestation about how democracy and tyranny differ. Why do some persist while others perish? How, why, and when do authoritarianism and anti-authoritarianism arise? How do power and tyranny work through formal institutions and everyday spheres from below? What are the possibilities for people to resist under these different political configurations? What forms of reclamation and abolition are urgently needed for community placemaking and collective movements to disrupt patterns of violence and injustice wrought, past and present, throughout the region? By examining these questions, the course speaks to some of the rising tensions and pressing contemporary issues facing Asian countries and beyond the region. Students will gain a textured and nuanced understanding of these important dynamics and timely subjects through seminal political writings, historical texts, and cultural materials, as well as films, music, comics, poetry, and fiction from East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.

title: Animal Ethics in Asia
description: Examines the relationships between humans and animals across Asia, exploring cosmological and cultural frameworks as well as modern debates. Examines perspectives from myth, literature, and religion, where ideas about animal symbolism emerge along with concepts of morality, violence, and spiritual kinship with animals. Discusses moral philosophy and critical animal studies, using these perspectives to ethically evaluate issues like animal sacrifice, wildlife trade, animal biotechnologies, zoonotic disease, companion animals, and the ethics of keeping pets and other forms of interspecies intimacy. Considers the impacts of urban expansion, conservation challenges, and the formation of emerging animal rights and justice movements across Asia. How do cultural practices, metaphors, and traditions shape attitudes towards animals? How do people balance economic and ethical responsibilities when it comes to labor, farming, breeding, public health, and environmental challenges?

title: History of Medicine in South Asia
description: Study primary and secondary sources to explore how South Asian societies have understood the ideas of health and well-being throughout history. We will consider a number of cases that illustrate uniquely South Asian conceptions of illness and physical dysfunction and the ways in which people in South Asia have attempted (and continue to attempt today) to heal bodies. Students will learn about the traditional healing systems of South Asia, including Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani, the basic components of each systems' ideas about disease pathology and treatment that have been used for centuries to heal illness, maintain good health, and, in some instances, aspire to a state of super-health that transcends the limitations of bodily existence altogether.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How have people in South Asian societies understood and expressed ideas about health and illness, medicine and healing throughout history, in literature, and religion?  How have ideas about wellbeing and illness driven therapeutics for ailing bodies and regimens to maintain fit bodies?  Who gets to make determinations about what is fitness and unfitness and, crucially, how to shape or treat them?  These are some of the big questions that will frame our studies this semester of healing traditions, or medicines, in South Asia.  We'll read about and reflect on ways the human body is presumed to relate to disease and how people experience, carry, and convey the experience of illness.  Together we will think about how sometimes illnesses function as metaphors for social categories that people value as well as occasionally fear, and we will explore how those metaphorical expressions reveal concerns about larger cultural norms and institutions that shape the contours of our lives, such as, sex and gender, class and caste, and ethics and religion, and more.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Weekly Lectures   in-person, 2x per week

input: History of Medicine in South Asia

title: Language in Japanese Society
description: Enhances knowledge of and sensitivity towards social factors that influence how Japanese language is used in different contexts. Topics include language standardization and policies, dialects, gender differences, multilingualism, translation, and impact of technology on language. In addition to discussing books and articles on these subject matters, engage in the collaborative analysis of actual examples of Japanese language use taken from everyday interactions, interviews, traditional and social media discourse, popular culture, and public signage, among others. Through this process, evaluate critically taken-for-granted beliefs and assumptions about the Japanese language and its users; examine how particular beliefs and assumptions have been established, maintained, and challenged; and make informed choices in adopting different styles of language and in positioning themselves in a Japanese speech community. Not open to students with credit for E ASIAN 358 prior to Fall 2019.

instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
First Half 
 	Introduction / Overview
 	Language standardization and dialects
 	Language and gender
 	Politeness and honorifics
 	Revitalization of endangered languages
 	Race, ethnicity, and language
Second Half
 	Role language / script variation
 	Translation
 	Linguistic landscape
 	Writing system and multimodality

Learning Activities 

1)	Online discussion (30%)	
	
2)	Class attendance & participation (20%)		
	
3)	Qualitative interview project  (25%)		
For the first small research project, you are expected to conduct a qualitative research interview with speakers of Japanese. Interviewees must have at least two years of experience in living/working in Japan. Questions to be asked during the interview should be related to the topics covered in the first half of the class.

4)	Language use analysis project  (25%)			
In the second project, you are expected to conduct a close analysis of actual use of language seen in different genres of spoken and written language. You can choose whatever material you find interesting and manageable (e.g., anime, manga, drama, games, film, TV show, TV commercials, Youtube videos, audio or video-recorded actual interaction, lyrics of popular songs, short stories, language textbooks, web sites, SNS messages, public signage, etc.).

title: Indian Writers Abroad: Literature, Diaspora and Globalization
description: Study of literature, drama, and film produced by authors of South Asian origin in Europe, North America, and the Caribbean. Course considers theories of diaspora, changing patterns of subcontinental migration, and relation of diasporic forms to the cultures of origin and adoption. Not open to students with credit for LCA 478 prior to Fall 2019.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course focuses on some notable novels and films produced in English by authors whose cultural origins lie in countries such as India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka, but who have emigrated to or grown up in the West (Britain, Canada, and the US). Novelists such as Salman Rushdie, Amitav Ghosh, Monica Ali, and Jhumpa Lahiri, and filmmakers such as Hanif Kureishi, Gurinder Chadha, and Mira Nair (Zohran Mamdani's mother!) have been major figures in world literature and cinema since the 1980s because their work offers entirely new kinds of narratives about immigrant experience in Western countries while also preserving memories of "home." By bringing this work into the classroom, the course offers students of literature and the humanities an opportunity to understand how portrayals of South Asian migrant life through the medium of English have revolutionized literary and visual cultures around the world.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Colonial and postcolonial migrations from the Indian subcontinent; the emergence of major immigrant Indian novelists and film-makers in English in the UK, US, and Canada; major themes in immigrant fiction and cinema; the relationships between "home" and "host" cultures; immigrant identity in relation to race, class, and gender.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Lecture, discussion, group work, presentations, papers, exams.
keywords: Western countries as "host cultures" for immigrant populations
nostalgia for "home cultures," race relations in countries of migration

title: Agent of Resistance in Asia
description: Advanced topics in Asian studies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Amidst rising authoritarianism, this course comparatively examines resistance against autocratization and people's resolve to push back and demand voice, visibility, and social justice in Asia. The course offers a contemporary and historical perspective on various forms and sites of resistance across Asia: from the rise of Gen Z protests across South and Southeast Asia to  social movements against martial law in South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines and Myanmar, "white paper protests  against Covid-19 lockdown in China to umbrella movements in Hong Kong, enforced disappearances in Kashmir to refugee-settler entanglements across archipelago of empires across Asian waters, and others.
The course focuses on the agency of those who contest power, domination, and social oppression in dictatorships as well as democracies. While providing students with a conceptual framework to understand power, regime types, contentious politics, and resistance, the course directs attention to the actual agents of resistance, their values, worldview, and the strategies they deploy in order to be heard. The course covers a wide range of actors including everyday citizens, students, writers, artists, singers, workers, and villagers, as well as individuals and groups that traverse the boundaries between state and society. Also central to the course is the study of everyday, micro-level forms of resistance that do not manifest in large-scale social movements or tumultuous mass protests but are nevertheless central to dynamics of political change.
Who and when are individuals and groups likely to become "agents of resistance ? Why do some take up resistance while others do not? How do social agents manifest their contention? To what extent is social resistance inherently anti-authoritarian? Why does social resistance matter? The course examines these questions across political regimes and social and cultural contexts in Asia, including but not limited to: China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Japan, India, Bangladesh, Burma, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, Cambodia and Vietnam. Readings draw on a wide range of texts from comparative politics, sociology, history, cultural anthropology, literature, arts and performance and personal accounts written by agents of resistance themselves. By pairing seminal theories and concepts with first-hand activists' accounts, poetry, films, performances, sounds, and indigenous voices, the course examines a number of themes relating to rights and social justice, including: land dispossession, migrant labor, patriarchy and gender, displacement and refugees, and, finally, academic freedom. Ultimately, students in the course will develop a deeply contextual understanding of the imperatives, dynamics, and precarity of resistance and the resolve of its agents in Asia.

title: Ethnography in Asia
description: From Greek ethnos, "folk" + grapho, "to write," doing ethnography involves writing about people, societies, and cultures. It is a qualitative, rather than a quantitative, type of research. One does ethnography, and thus it's a process.  But an ethnography is also a product: the outcome of the ethnographic process is an ethnography. In-depth studies and discussions of classic and contemporary ethnographies in multiple Asian contexts that focus on themes like religion, health, economics, and sexuality in writing, photography, and film at once illustrate various methods involved in doing ethnography and illuminate why scholars have for decades studied and represented Asia through ethnography. The methods of ethnography are never divorced from the motivations of the scholars, and thus it is crucial to probe critically and collectively what ethnography is (theory), how it is done (practice), and why is it worth doing generally and in Asian contexts in particular.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: From Greek ethnos ("population group") + grapho ("to write"), ethnography traditionally has involved observing and then writing about people, societies, and cultures. Historically, ethnography has primarily involved qualitative rather than quantitative research, although these two methods can be and often are combined in ethnographies across disciplines. This semester we will think about how people do ethnography, and thus consider ethnography as a process, in Asian contexts. We will also think about ethnography as a product (i.e., the outcome of ethnographic research is an ethnography, or an ethnographic study).  Which is to say, we will read, watch, and discuss ethnography as both method and product in several Asian societies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: What is mindfulness? How is it practiced? And why has it become so popular? These and other questions will animate our examination of mindfulness in both theoretical and practical terms. Drawing on materials ranging from Buddhist Studies to Cognitive Science, we will first inquire into the basic theories that underlie the development of mindfulness in its original Buddhist context. The course then turns to the contemporary transformation and application of mindfulness in psychology, business, health care and beyond. We will explore how mindfulness has changed in these contexts in ways that increase its cultural appeal. And we will likewise examine contemporary scientific accounts of mindfulness as an object of research, especially as a means to promote flourishing. This course will include opportunities for students to explore mindfulness experientially through meditative practice.

title: Prokaryotic Molecular Biology
description: Molecular basis of bacterial physiology and genetics with emphasis on molecular mechanisms; topics include nucleic acid-protein interactions, transcription, translation, replication, recombination, regulation of gene expression.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
An advanced course in molecular biology of prokaryotes, Microbio/Biochem/Genetics 612 builds on the knowledge gained in [Biochem 501 or 507] AND [Microbio 470 or Genetics 466 or 468] 

The content focuses on our present understanding of molecular mechanisms obtained from biochemical, structural, and genetic approaches as well as experimental methods that reveal this information. Both foundational studies in "model"  systems and non-model examples will be discussed.

The course will emphasize experimental methods, data analysis, and discussion of primary literature. Course modules will address core molecular biology concepts such as fidelity, specificity, plasticity, and spatial and temporal organization through topics including replication, topology, repair, gene expression, translation, regulatory networks, signaling, horizontal gene transfer, cellular defense systems, protein secretion, and bacteriophage.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
Examples listed below are topics covered in recent years (some will change based on current literature):
- how is timing of replication initiation regulated at the molecular level?
- how does replication stop on a circular chromosome?
- how do polymerases accommodate damaged nucleotides?
- how does RNA polymerase respond to promoter sequences and transition to active transcription?
- how do coupling of transcription and translation affect gene expression in bacteria?
- how do alarmones regulate gene expression?
- how to small RNAs impact gene regulation?
- how do bacteria integrate environmental cues to regulate genes appropriately?
- how does the 3D nature of the chromosome impact gene expression?
- how do RNA and protein degradation impact gene expression?
- how are macromolecules organized in cells lacking organelles?
- how do bacteria and phage counteract each other? (CRISPR is not only about genetic engineering!)
- how does horizontal gene transfer impact gene regulation in bacteria?

Topics are covered using primary literature to discuss our evolving understanding of these and other prokaryotic molecular biology topics. Advances come from studies ranging from classical methods to state-of-the-art analyses such as cryo-EM and computational tools.
instructorProvidedContent.format:
In-person attendance is required. Mix of lectures, problem solving/experimental design, and group discussions of primary literature. 

Assessment is based on individual responses to content questions,  literature discussions, and presentations.

This is a upper level undergraduate/graduate level course. Students are expected to review prerequisite course material independently and access library resources to fill their knowledge gaps.

title: Responsible Conduct in Bioscience Research
description: Introductory training in the practical aspects of being a graduate-level scientist and the professional standards and expectations of ethical researchers. Covers a wide variety of professional development topics, including choosing a research laboratory and a thesis mentor, transitioning to self-education, managing stress in graduate school, and the importance of diversity in science. Ethics topics include conflicts of interest, the protection of human subjects, the welfare of laboratory animals and workers, safe laboratory spaces, mentor and mentee responsibilities, collaborative research, peer review, data acquisition and data management practices, research misconduct, responsible authorship and publication, contemporary ethical issues in biomedical research, and the roles of responsible scientists in society. Covers all NIH-recommended topics for Responsible Conduct of Research, thus meeting the requirements for trainees involved in NIH-sponsored research programs.

title: Synthetic Biology Seminar
description: Synthetic biology is a burgeoning field encompassing understanding and designing biological systems spanning from biomolecules to ecosystems. It builds on advances in molecular and cellular technologies to revolutionize biological engineering in the same way that organic synthesis transformed chemistry and integrated circuit design transformed computing. Synthetic biology has the potential to address many of society's grand challenges including: understanding human disease, sustainable biomanufacturing, medical diagnostics and therapeutics, programming mammalian cell behaviors, engineering living materials, information storage, carbon sequestration, and energy generation. Latest advances in the field will be reviewed by covering literature including but not limited to biomolecular design, sequence-structure-function relationship, regulatory and signaling networks, metabolic engineering, interactions in microbial communities, cell-based therapeutics and genome design.

title: Communicating Evolutionary Biology
description: Exposure to diverse topics in contemporary evolutionary biology and development of critical thinking and communication skills. Most weeks guest lecturers present their own primary research on a specialized topic in evolutionary biology. Seminars include perspectives from genetics, ecology, geoscience, zoology, botany, microbiology, systematics, molecular biology, and integrative research. Some weeks feature special topics and discussions on pedagogical, legal, outreach, or other issues in evolutionary biology. Includes thinking critically about methodology, experimental design and interpretation, and how conclusions are reached in evolutionary biology by reading primary and secondary literature, attending seminars, discussing topics with speakers and other students, and preparing a written report.  The 3-credit version of the course delves deeper into communication of evolutionary biology to researchers, undergraduates, K-12 students, and the general public.

title: Survey of Quality Assurance and Regulatory Affairs in Biotechnology
description: Success in the biotechnology industry is based on learning the language and understanding the development process utilized in bringing products to market. Focus on techniques used in the biotechnology industry to comply with the quality and regulatory requirements set forth by professional and governmental agencies in the effort to develop, manufacture, and commercialize products safely for the public.

input: Survey of Quality Assurance and Regulatory Affairs in Biotechnology

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Intellectual Property, Patents and Licensing
description: Explore core concepts of how intellectual property, patent law, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, licensing and patent litigation specifically relate to the field of biotechnology. Evaluate how types of intellectual property work to protect a product or service. Explain the importance of patents in terms of licensing and technology transfer. Assess the unique aspects of early-stage intellectual property, including how it pertains to market dynamics, pricing and valuation.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Biotechnology Regulation and Ethics
description: Explore political, legal, and ethical issues and paradigms that drive product development within the biotechnology industry with special emphasis given to how new drugs, devices, and biologics are regulated by local, national, and global agencies. Describe the regulations and ethics of human subjects' research. Develop skills to support how regulation and politics interact with business and finance to influence the formation and growth of biotechnology companies. Discuss how ethics and regulatory policy influence how biotechnology products come to market.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Business of Biotechnology: Business Fundamentals
description: Discover the business challenges inherent in translating scientific discoveries into a successful business. Apply fundamental business principles that guide the operations of biotechnology companies.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Molecular Technologies I: Diagnostic Testing
description: Assess various biotechnology techniques to determine effective and efficient methods used in biotechnology product development. Utilize analytical and  communication skills when critiquing biotechnology applications that simulate both corporate and academic biotechnology settings.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Early Drug Discovery
description: Examine the early drug discovery process, including target identification and validation, generation of diverse chemical libraries, assay development and high throughput screening, lead optimization by compound profiling, and drug targeting and delivery.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Business of Biotechnology: Commercialization Pathways
description: Explore contemporary issues in the business of biotechnology and apply concepts critical to the success of modern biotechnology firms. Focus on modern problem-solving topics, including issues relating to corporate leadership, fundings sources for product development, customer identification, financial accounting management, and negotiation.

schoolCollege.formalDescription: Medicine and Public Health, School of

title: Molecular Technologies III: Assay Development
description: Evaluate laboratory assays and methods used in primary, secondary, and in vitro ADMETox (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, Toxicity) drug screening. Build scientific  communication and critical thinking skills while working on team projects and analyzing scientific results.

description: Self-directed work under the supervision and guidance of an Instructor and often in conjunction with a day-to-day mentor that is a graduate student or postdoc researcher in the instructor's group. Students normally participate in aspects of ongoing research projects.

title: Practical Biophysics
description: Introduction to methods used in biophysical measurements. Thermodynamics and kinetics are introduced along with the theory and instrumentation used for several complementary biophysical approaches. Hands-on experimentation using state-of-the-art instrumentation and data interpretation.

title: Responsible Conduct in Bioscience Research
description: Introductory training in the practical aspects of being a graduate-level scientist and the professional standards and expectations of ethical researchers. Covers a wide variety of professional development topics, including choosing a research laboratory and a thesis mentor, transitioning to self-education, managing stress in graduate school, and the importance of diversity in science. Ethics topics include conflicts of interest, the protection of human subjects, the welfare of laboratory animals and workers, safe laboratory spaces, mentor and mentee responsibilities, collaborative research, peer review, data acquisition and data management practices, research misconduct, responsible authorship and publication, contemporary ethical issues in biomedical research, and the roles of responsible scientists in society. Covers all NIH-recommended topics for Responsible Conduct of Research, thus meeting the requirements for trainees involved in NIH-sponsored research programs.

title: Rainforests and Coral Reefs
description: Are you awed by the amazing biodiversity found in rainforests and coral reefs? See these ecosystems first hand and decide if a career in tropical biology or international conservation is for you. Focuses on the ecology of the world's most biodiverse ecosystems, and their global importance. Learn the physical, chemical, and biological processes that make rainforests and coral reefs function, and the history of human dependence upon these ecosystems. Understand why both of these ecosystems currently are threatened and what actions can and must be taken to protect them.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Botany 330 is an organismal biology course that focuses on photosynthetic protists and bacteria, particularly species relevant to human health and sustainability. For undergraduate students this capstone-like course builds on previous biology and chemistry background to foster readiness for graduate study or the biology-related workplace. Graduate students gain expertise fundamental to plant evolutionary biology, water sciences, and emerging industrial applications.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
The first two weeks link previous knowledge of photosynthesis, plant nutrition, global mineral cycling, symbiosis, food web ecology, and evolutionary biology to the solution of societal issues such as water pollution and renewable energy. Early lab and field experiences provide fundamental techniques in microscopy, microbiology, microbial enumeration, molecular biology and imaging that students use to pursue individual interests.
The middle portion of the course provides hands-on experience with major groups of freshwater, marine, and terrestrial photosynthetic protists and bacteria, supported by reading, writing, and oral presentation experiences.
The course concludes with ecological work that builds on previous course material.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Blended learning. Students use a personal copy of an up-to-date digital textbook to prepare for each in-person lab session, guided by worksheets posted weekly on Canvas. Completion of worksheets will be done individually, not in collaboration. Students will turn in worksheets by specified weekly deadlines, to Canvas. Worksheet feedback (including grades) will be posted there.

title: The North American West to 1850
description: Explores the history of places that have been called the American West before 1850. We start with Indigenous occupation; continue with European invasion and the creation of two new nations, Mexico and the U.S.; and end with U.S. conquest. We watch Indian lands becoming the object of Spanish, French, and English empires, and then see European incursions giving way to the hopes of new nation-states and newly empowered Indian peoples like Lakotas and Comanches. After studying the trails and trades that brought newcomers west, we reach key converging events: U.S. seizure of the Mexican North, resolution of the Oregon boundary dispute, discovery of western gold, West Coast arrival of Chinese immigrants, and Mormon exodus to the Great Basin. We use economic, environmental, political, cultural, and social analyses, and we attend to the dreams of many westerners: of North American, Latin American, European, African, and Asian origin or descent, and of all genders and class statuses.

title: Latina/Latino/Latinx History
description: Examines the historical, social, and legal experiences of Latinas/Latinos/Latinxs in the US since the mid-1800s with emphasis on Mexican migrations. Latinxs became an important part of the US population through western expansion, conquest, and immigration. We will learn about the 3 main Latinx groups in the US: Mexicans, Puerto Ricans, and Cubans, but will also learn about other Latinx communities. We begin with an examination of conquest by studying the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo that annexed roughly half of former Mexican territory and the Spanish-American War that resulted in the possession of Puerto Rico. Then, we examine the history of Latinx immigration to understand the experiences of Mexicans, Central Americans, South Americans, and people from the Caribbean who have immigrated to the US in search of economic opportunities and political asylum. This course serves as an introduction to the varied experiences of Latinxs in the US in order to understand their unique histories.

title: Chicanx/e and Latinx/e Education in the U.S.
description: Political, historical, and cultural analysis of Chicanx/e, Mexican American, and Latinx/e students' experiences in K-12 education in the United States. Examines how educational policies, programs, and practices shape schooling experiences and educational outcomes for these populations. Emphasizes an intersectional framework that moves beyond explanations centered solely on language background or immigrant status. Draws on schooling and educational histories to develop a sociohistorical understanding of public education in the U.S.

description: Explores photographic archives and photography-based aesthetic projects that reflect on the experiences of the Latinx, Caribbean, Latin American and AfroAmerican experience. description: Develop an understanding of immigrant health in the United States from the perspective of social and structural determinants. title: Survey of Latinx/e Popular Culture
description: Analysis of Latinx/e popular culture to consider the varied make-up of Latinx/e populations, their specific histories, social dynamics, and politics through their creative expressions, performances, and cultural contestations. Covers key terms and concepts, cultural developments, and diverse interpretations while focusing in the analysis of Latinx/e music, performance art, film and media, sports, food, and car culture. Other topics include the production, circulation, and reception of Latinx/e popular culture, the use of Spanish and English languages, issues of identity, migration, and interculturality, the role of the cultural industry, and the context of globalization. Broadly explores the intersectionality of race, ethnicity, class, gender, sexuality, and nation regarding Latinx/e populations. Taught in Spanish.

title: Black and Latinx in Literature and Visual Culture
description: Chicanxs and Latinxs are frequently imagined in ways that erase the history, presence, and influence of African-descended peoples within these groups. However, this anti-Blackness does not go unanswered in Chicanx and Latinx cultural production. Covers literature, life-writing/autoethnography, visual culture, philosophy/theory, and history that takes up Black Latinx experience and/or that comparatively explores the African American and Latinx convergences, exploring a rich vein of thought and representation in U.S. literatures that is often more transamerican than American and that offers new definitions of both Latinx and Black. Readings on racial paradigms in the Americas, paying attention to the differences between US and Latin American contexts, as well readings on decoloniality, intersectional feminisms, borderlands, and diaspora.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: African diaspora populations and their cultural and literary expression are significant throughout the Americas. This interdisciplinary course explores literature and film about the intersection of Black and Latinx in the U.S. as well as the transnational dimensions of Black Latinidades across the Americas. We will study literatures, theory/philosophy, histories, autoethnography/testimonio, and visual cultures.    Assignments will include regular short writing assignments about our readings and films, in-class discussions and exercises, quizzes, and exams.

title: Ancient Greek and Roman Monsters
description: Ancient monsters were forces of chaos that threatened the natural order of the universe: they had to be contained, banished to the edges of the world or destroyed. But the Greeks and Romans also believed them to be magical beings that held the promise of special knowledge - of the past, of dangers to be faced, of musical arts - or which, like the Sphinx, possessed an enigmatic intelligence capable of fooling all but the most cunning of mortals. Investigate these contrasting aspects of ancient monsters, drawing directly on texts (in translation) and works of art through which the Greeks and Romans explored the monstrous and its place in their world. Compare ancient representations with those in modern artistic media - comics, games, stories and movies - considering both how our notions of the monstrous are influenced by or contrast with those of our ancient predecessors, and how our very identities are created by and enacted through our depictions of monsters.

title: Slavery in the Ancient Roman World
description: Slavery pervaded every part of life in ancient Greece and Rome. As the influential historian of the ancient economy Moses Finley put it, "there was no action or belief or institution in Greco-Roman antiquity that was not one way or other affected by the possibility that someone involved might be a slave." Focuses on slavery in ancient Rome, with due attention given to comparative material (Near Eastern, Greek, and Atlantic). Provides an overview of the institution and its role in Roman private and public life, and examines a variety of evidence (literary, material, documentary) that confronts important themes in the study of ancient slavery, e.g. ideologies of slavery and freedom; manumission; the social position of enslaved and freed people; gender, sexuality, and the family; literary depictions of slavery; and comparative slaveries.

title: Argumentation and Debate
description: Develop your skills of argument to productively engage people in a diverse society. Learn to discuss differences with others and to contribute positively to a dynamic and diverse society. Critically examine the roles of advocates and audience members. Gain an understanding of the contexts and significance of argument in democratic societies, identity the components and qualities of arguments, construct cogent ethical arguments, and evaluate the arguments of others.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Develop your skills of argument to productively engage people in a diverse society. Learn to discuss differences with others. Examine the roles of advocates and audience members. Gain an understanding of the contexts and significance of argument in democratic societies, identify the components and qualities of arguments, construct cogent ethical arguments, and evaluate the arguments of others.


Overview
This course seeks to prepare students with the skills to interpret and construct arguments in the everyday contexts of social and political dialogue about matters of shared concern. Taking this approach, this course confronts two disabling commonplace views of argument. The first view asserts that all arguments are opinions that cannot be debated or judged; thus, all arguments are equally acceptable (e.g., "You have your opinion, I have mine,"  or "It's all just opinion") and incapable of support. This course counters that arguments can be advanced with good and bad reasons, with sufficient and insufficient support. The second view fails to recognize that cogent reasons can be offered for positions different than one's own. This course retorts that because we live in a pluralistic society of diverse values and beliefs, we need to recognize the legitimacy of opposing viewpoints. Disagreement in such instances need not always be seen as an error in reasoning or lack of evidence. Yet, valuing the view of another requires us to take arguments seriously and evaluate their cogency. This task appears especially difficult in our contemporary society as political polarization reigns and differences are demonized. This course starts with the basic belief that we must be able to discuss our differences and that these differences can be generative and productive in a dynamic and diverse society. Starting from this faith, we will learn skills and perspectives that we can use to foster a democratic society. 

The skills of argument reference our roles as advocates and audience members. As advocates, we need to construct arguments and engage others in processes of argumentation. We may argue in numerous contexts in formal and informal settings, online and offline, with strangers and family members. In all of these contexts, we may argue about personal matters, such as who washed the dishes last, and public matters that concern us collectively, such as whether to rename campus buildings or how we should regulate artificial intelligence. This course focuses on our role as advocates of public argument. Even so, we may encounter argumentation more as audiences than as advocates when we see advertisements, or consider different perspectives on social protest, or reflect on changing norms about proper professional conduct. As audience members, we need to engage these arguments critically, and, when necessary, we need to be prepared to act as advocates in response to the arguments we encounter.

Assignments typically include exams, participation, papers, and speeches.

1.	Map how the idea of democracy has shifted and evolved throughout US history.

title: The Power of the Image
description: Explore various topics in rhetoric, politics, and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Images surround us today they are on our televisions and magazines, our phones and social media feeds, on street-side billboards and in the artwork we consume. There's no escaping the fact that images have power and shape how we live and engage with the world. This course is designed to help students understand what images do for and to us, as well as what we do with images. We will cover a range of theoretical approaches, texts and media to examine how images make meaning. We will learn how to read and interpret a variety of image forms including, but not limited to advertising images, news photographs, political posters, short-videos and memes. In doing so, we will learn how images impact our relationship to the world in all its complexity how they mediate questions of race and gender, how images reflect and shape politics, and how images can be repurposed and remixed to make sense of the world as individuals, and to imagine collective futures.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, you will be able to:
- Understand the historical and social significance factors behind the emergence of 20th and 21st century visual culture 
- Analyze the technological and aesthetic aspects of visual culture
- Develop a keen understanding of the relationship between visuality, rhetoric and power
- Understand how visual forms can give expression to various aspects of the human condition and generate public discourse

title: Pop Music Cinema
description: Explore various topics in film and media studies, history, and theory.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Pop Music Cinema traces the cultural history of the U.S. recording industry through critical analysis of films about popular music. Each week, a feature-length film anchors our exploration of how the music industry represents itself on screen, providing a lens for examining themes such as stardom, genre formation, technological change, and institutional power. By pairing film analysis with media industry history, the course reveals how popular music's cultural meaning is constructed, contested, and circulated through the moving image.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
Below is an outline of the key topics and a selection of screenings for that unit (subject to change): 

Unit 1 will introduce key frameworks of textual analysis, such as narrative, mise-en-sc ne, cinematography, and editing. Screenings during this unit include Trolls World Tour (2020), The Girl Can't Help It (1956), and Gimme Shelter (1970). 

Unit 2 will explore different film genres as narrative blueprints that enable filmmakers to critique key aspects of popular music culture, such as the recording industry, technology, and identity. Screenings during this unit include Sinners (2025), Phantom of the Paradise (1974), and Josie and the Pussycats (2001). 

Unit 3 will examine the storytelling properties of non-fiction music films, such as biopics and documentaries, to interrogate the politics of representing real-life artists and scenes. Screenings during this unit include 24 Hour Party People (2002), Pavements (2024), and Charli XCX: Alone Together (2021).

title: Television's Greatest Hits
description: Explore various topics in film and media studies, history, and theory.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
In one form or another, television has now existed for almost 100 years. What is the best that it has given American society and culture in this time? This course examines the "greatest hits  of the medium, shows that have risen above the normal or everyday, whether in artistic achievement, in cultural impact, in sheer popularity, or in novelty and importance. The exact lineup of shows under consideration will be determined with student preferences and interests in mind, ranging across genres, but will include Sesame Street, Game of Thrones, Lost, The Daily Show, The Simpsons, South Park, I Love Lucy, Twilight Zone, Stranger Things, Squid Game, and more. In each case, we'll consider how the program changed the structure and business of television, how its style, messages, aesthetics, and stories mattered, and who it mattered to. Whether you love and know your greatest hits well, would appreciate a primer, or are trying to cover up some gaps here and there, all are welcome. We'll discuss the shows intensely, draw connections, and along the way consider the bigger questions of what television should do for American society, what we've asked it to do and what more it could do, how different genres work and matter, what it even means to call something "great  or a "hit,  and how the medium has evolved (as technological, industrial, and aesthetic system), with particular interest in the current era.

Note: Students are not restricted to taking only one CA 313: these are special topic classes, and hence you can take several for credit.

title: Music Industries and Popular Culture
description: The popular music industries are a vital part of the media industries. Music is the soundtrack to our lives. It provides the score to our quietest moments alone and our loudest parties with friends. Music helps us create and understand our identities and those of others. It is both a form of subversive activism and one of the most commercially valuable commodities in the media industries. Explore the contemporary popular music industries and the roles businesses, artists, audiences, fans, and technologies play in shaping music as a media industry. Focus specifically on the disruption that the internet, digital technologies, and social media have ushered in over the last two decades and the new ways artists, listeners, and businesses are discovering, promoting, sharing and experiencing music. Talk about the music you love, how it gets made, and why that matters for how we understand creative industries, ourselves, and each other.

title: Television Industries
description: Critical overview of the cultural industries driving television in the United States, from broadcast networks and cable to downloading and streaming, focusing on economic and regulatory structures, programming practices, labor, globalization, audiences, and adaptations to changing conditions in the digital age.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This course will introduce you to the study of the industries that produce, distribute, and deliver television in a "post-network  era, considering television programs as meaningful cultural objects produced by a specific set of industrial institutions. Focusing on commercial television in the United States, but offering comparisons to global and non-commercial alternatives, we will explore television in terms of the market logics, programming traditions, and cultures of production all under transformation by emerging digital platforms and patterns of media use. Whether you imagine your future engagements with television as a producer, or consumer, or concerned citizen, the course should prepare you to engage more critically with the television industries and encourage you to consider how the status quo might be usefully challenged.

Learning is typically assessed through a research project, participation, and active learning exercises.

Course learning outcomes:
1)	describe the economic, technological, and regulatory pressures reshaping American television
2)	evaluate television programming as a complex form of cultural production with its own set of aesthetics, constraints, and conventions
3)	critically examine the hierarchies of power that shape identity, community, and inclusion in television production cultures
4)	develop strong arguments about industry through sustained research and analysis of trade journals and other primary evidence
5)	use feedback to improve critical insights about industry through the process of revision
6)	apply industry principles of long-term planning, development, and scheduling to course work

title: Sound Cultures: Podcasting and Music
description: Sound plays a crucial but understudied role in experiences of media and cultural life. From the mundane sounds of our daily routines to the irresistible refrains of our favorite songs, sound (in its various guises as noise, music, echo, vibration, etc.) is fundamental to communications media and, more broadly, to our perceptions of the world around us. An introduction to the emerging field of sound studies and an investigation into the role sound and music (or lack thereof) play in various communications media. Through audio assignments such as the creation of podcasts, learn the basics of digital audio recording and editing software and how to present and distribute audio content via the Internet, specifically as podcasts. Gain practical skills for creating digital audio projects and a deeper appreciation for how paying attention to sound leads to unique understandings of history, culture, and media technologies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Sound plays a crucial but understudied role in experiences of media and cultural life. From the mundane sounds of our daily routines (a bus lumbering by, water dripping from a faucet, the clack of a keyboard, etc.) to more structured and constructed soundworks (i.e. radio, music, sound for television, film, and games, etc.), sound, or lack thereof, is fundamental to communications media and, more broadly, to our perceptions of the world around us. This class aims to introduce you to the field of sound studies, an emerging sub-discipline within media studies that takes sound as its primary focus. We'll consider the role sound plays in various communications media through topics such as: soundscapes and the way sounds affect our understanding of urban and other spaces, music and the ordering of sound for commercial and aesthetic ends, deafness and silence, listening in an era of digital sound, video game sound, and technologies of sound production, like artificial intelligence. You will also put these theories into practice through audio assignments such as the creation of podcasts and other brief soundworks. You will learn the basics of digital audio recording and editing software and how to present and distribute amateur/everyday audio content via the Internet, specifically as podcasts. By the end of this class, you will have both practical skills for creating digital audio projects and theoretical concepts for answering questions around what it might mean to think sonically and to be sound students. You'll also have an overview of the podcasting industry, and how new technologies, like AI, are affecting the industry.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: We will take "new media" to mean primarily, though not exclusively, digital media. As part of the course, we will examine how this label of "newness" has been applied in various sociotechnical contexts. Specifically, we will examine the role of digital media in collecting, aggregating, and visualizing geolocative data. Case studies for this course include Tinder's data-collection and interface design, Amazon Ring surveillance cameras, and Uber's surge-pricing algorithms. This critical approach to media infrastructure will lead to a deeper understanding of how digital media is not just cloud-based or placeless but supported by a vast network of underwater cables, data centers, and Bluetooth sensors embedded in everyday technologies.

title: Rhetoric and Power on the Internet
description: Explores and analyzes Internet communication as a magnifier, transmitter, and limiter of power for both individual people and institutions with special attention to the roles of politics, social issues, and justice. Use rhetorical analysis to engage in the critical assessment of Internet media content that exerts power in their lives.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
The rise of the internet as our primary site for public life and political discourse has dramatically changed the ways in which power is negotiated today. From Arab Spring to Black Lives Matter, from #MeToo to January 6th, online social movements have used social media and the internet as a site for collective organizing and mobilization. At the same time, conspiracy theories and mis/disinformation spread across the internet putting serious pressure on civic norms, often accelerated by foreign adversaries who seek to undermine democracy with civil unrest and discord. In this course, we will navigate and analyze emerging rhetorical, ideological, and political dynamics on the internet, focusing on emerging political configurations, opportunities, mobilizations, and threats. We will theorize the current state of the internet through focused engagement with critical and rhetorical theory, and we will map the (re)territorialization of power structures online.

Course objectives:
1.	Understand the role of the internet in navigating and maintaining power relations
2.	Analyze the role of rhetoric in shaping power relations online
3.	Recognize the importance of the internet for activism, politics, conspiracism, and extremism
4.	Articulate the possibilities for technological interventions in existing political formations
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
This course will cover current events and topics related to online extremism, activism, and politics as mediated by the internet and social media. Topics include:

1. The internet as a site for navigating power imbalances and relations.
2. Social media as an organizing tool for activist groups such as Anonymous and Arab Spring.
3. Rhetorics of power as mediated or accelerated by information technology.
4. The growth and spread of online conspiracism and extremism through internet infrastructure.
5. Alternative sites of power relations such as the "dark web."
6. Emerging political instabilities accelerated by the internet such as "information warfare."
7. The use of the internet as a site for intelligence gathering.
8. Institutional norms and rhetorics about the emergence of AI.
9. Institutional communications through social media.
10. Mapping the territories of power online.

title: Rhetoric of Globalization and Transnationalism
description: Introduction to basic concepts in global and transnational rhetorical studies and provided with the analytic tools to examine discourses about globalization and transnationalism produced by key global actors including transnational corporations, states, global institutions such as the World Bank, media producers, human rights advocates, and activists.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Globalization is frequently thought of as an area of scholarly inquiry for economists and political scientists, but this course demonstrates that rhetorical and cultural studies approaches offer useful tools for examining the messages, motivations, movements, and mobilizations of globalization. The course will begin by introducing students to the basic elements of globalization and its influence in social, cultural, economic, and political life. We will address the rhetorical moves and investments of key global actors including transnational corporations, states, global economic and political governance institutions, human rights advocates, and activists. We will also pay attention to the way media structures our perceptions of the global and the local. Each module focuses on a conceptual theme that is aimed at broadening our horizons of understanding the meanings of "the global  and "the local.  What do ethnic and political identities look like in a world that is increasingly mobile and interconnected? How do globalization and transnationalism modify our conceptions of "the other  and what functions do cinema, television and the internet perform in this reconceptualization? By asking these questions, we will collectively attempt to understand what it means to live in a world marked by increasing contact between different peoples, their languages and their cultures.

Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

o	Understand key theories, concepts, debates, and methodologies used to explain and analyze globalization and transnationalism
o	Synthesize the predominant rhetorics of globalization
o	Evaluate and assess the message strategies of key global actors and institutions including nation-state heads, global governance institutions, transnational corporations, international legal bodies, human rights actors, activists, and people themselves.
o	Comprehend the role and effects of representation and power as it pertains to a globally connected world

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This graduate seminar will explore the institutions and agents of film culture from the 1930s to the present. We will investigate film festivals, cinematheques, museums, universities, funding institutions, civic groups, and political movements in terms of their impact on film culture. Our research questions will include: How have scholars analyzed the most proximate cultural mechanisms surrounding movies? What is the shifting nature of cinephilia in the U.S., Europe, and Latin America? How does film taste change over time? What are some of the relationships between film culture and political movements? How and when did film studies enter higher education? When and how did film enter museums?  Why did some post-revolutionary governments (in Cuba and Algeria, for example) take the time to create cinematheques? Why was the 2021 launch of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures so controversial? Why was Madison a hotbed of cinephilia in the 1960s and 70s? How has Letterboxd contributed to film culture? More broadly, how have scholars approached film culture at the local, regional, national, or transnational levels? 

Readings will include Haidee Wasson's Museum Movies: The Museum of Modern Art and the Birth of Art Cinema , Aurore Spiers's Archiving the Past: Women's Film History in France, 1927--1978, Colin Burnett's The Invention of Robert Bresson: the Auteur and his Market, Rielle Navitski's Transatlantic Cinephilia: Film Culture between Latin America and France, 1945--1965, and Dana Polan's Scenes of Instruction: The Beginnings of the U.S. Study of Film. We will also draw on key readings about the writing of cultural history by figures such as Carlo Ginzberg, Michael Baxandall, and Pierre Bourdieu.

title: Activating Ecological Society
description: Work toward an ecological society, where organizations and organizers create the conditions for mutually beneficial relationships across species, social space, and time. Discover tools that help you to activate ecological society. Identify communities to work with and your best role. Learn how to navigate power structures to make change and how to weave together different ways of knowing. Reframe problems into questions, use processes for consensus building, and galvanize dissent into purpose. Develop competency in identifying predominant organizations (for-profit, non-profit, and cutting-edge entities such as community trusts). Create an action portfolio demonstrating an ability to activate ecological society.

instructorProvidedContent.format: This class will alternate between discussions and workshops weekly. You will receive feedback on ungraded weekly portfolio activities in class every Tuesday, following the presentation and workshopping of new materials the prior week. Within a small group each Tuesday, you will present your assignment from that week. Based on instructor feedback and that of your peers, you will be required to revise your work based on this weekly feedback and submit a second version as part of your portfolio, due three times over the course of the semester. These revised weekly activities build into an action portfolio centered around a community of your choosing. You will leave this course with an action portfolio that you are proud of and can thumb through for years to come, as it hopefully helps you facilitate future action in communities.

title: Education for Sustainable Communities
description: How can education - for children and adults, in school and out - help to address crucial environmental and social sustainability challenges? What ideas and strategies have guided environmental and sustainability education over the years? What can individual people do to address environmental challenges, and what can only be accomplished by people working together? What does sustainability have to do with justice - and vice versa? Examine the principles behind behavior change and empowerment, community action and whole-scale social reform. Drawing on research and theory from across the social sciences, we will explore the uncertain relationship between education and advocacy, seeking the means by which education can have the greatest impact without compromising the core ideals of a democratic society.

title: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in Latin American society and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Brazil has long inspired curiosity in intellectual and artistic outsiders: from Michel de Montaigne's inauguration of the modern essay ("Of Cannibals,  1580) to Claude Levi-Strauss' notorious "writing lessons  in Tristes Tropiques (1955) to Michel Foucault's emergent theories of power in the 1970s and into Global Black studies of the 21st century. This interdisciplinary graduate seminar analyzes how Brazil   the place as well as the idea; the former colony and nation-state, as well as its representations   generates theory. Encounters and clashes among strikingly different peoples and worldviews shape how intellectuals and artists, both foreign and national, understand Brazil. Its staggering heterogeneity -- from pre-conquest cosmologies and especially beginning with the profoundly unequal European-Indigenous-African contact zones in the 15th and 16th centuries   makes it a singular incubator to understand theory as an inquiry into how knowledge grapples with what is new, unfamiliar, or unthinkable to it, as a perpetual search for knowledge in modernity, in worlds of mixture, conflict, and difference. The frequent motif of Brazil as a puzzle to both foreigners and Brazilians alike is perhaps best captured in political theorist Francisco de Oliveira's (2003) memorable metaphor of the duckbilled platypus, a walking paradox: at once reptile, bird, mammal - all three or none of these. In this course, we will trace how a Brazil imagined   "in theory,  in our everyday language, means an untested hypothesis   is also a story about what theory is and does. We will read theoretical essays by Brazilian and international thinkers and analyze works of the visual and literary arts from Brazil as aesthetic theory. The course will be of special interest to students of postcolonial or decolonial thought and Latin American/Caribbean studies. No knowledge of Brazil or Latin America is required. Students with reading knowledge of Portuguese will be encouraged to read in the original language.

title: Programming II
description: Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming using classes and objects to solve more complex problems. Introduces array-based and linked data structures: including lists, stacks, and queues. Programming assignments require writing and developing multi-class (file) programs using interfaces, generics, and exception handling to solve challenging real world problems. Topics reviewed include reading/writing data and objects from/to files and exception handling, and command line arguments. Topics introduced: object-oriented design; class vs. object; create and define interfaces and iterators; searching and sorting; abstract data types (List,Stack,Queue,PriorityQueue(Heap),Binary Search Tree); generic interfaces (parametric polymorphism); how to design and write test methods and classes; array based vs. linked node implementations; introduction to complexity analysis; recursion.

description: An introduction to fundamental structures of computer systems and the C programming language with a focus on the low-level interrelationships and impacts on performance. title: Software Engineering
description: Ideas and techniques for designing, developing, and modifying large software systems. Topics include software engineering processes; requirements and specifications; project team organization and management; software architectures; design patterns; testing and debugging; and cost and quality metrics and estimation. Work in large teams on a substantial programming project.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
PHYSICAL ATTENDANCE in class accounts for approximately 20% of the CS506 grade.
Students are required to commit to working closely with their teams. Grades depend substantially on participation; this includes:
* attendance/participation in in-class project activities
* regular participation in group development sessions
* weekly 20-minute zoom team meetings outside of class with an assigned TA.
A large team project (~12 weeks) is ONE emphasis of the course
* Projects are selected from a list created/provided by the instructors
* Teams are assigned: Students do not self-select their teams.
Exams:
* An in-person mid-term exam worth ~5% of the course grade
* An in-person final exam worth ~20% of the course grade
* An in-person "practical exam" in which the student demonstrates familiarity with a specific set of tools.

CS506 emphasizes student practice of software engineering technique. Students are assigned to teams of ~6; the bulk of the coursework comprises development of software within those teams, primarily on one major project lasting ~ twelve weeks.
Teams use Agile/Scrum methods to organize and manage their Team Project, while learning and applying various principles of software development/engineering, and working with several SWE technologies and tools (including: Git ; GitLab ; Docker ; MySQL ; MySQLWorkbench ; Mockito ; Postman ; SpringBoot)

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Topic Title: AI-Assisted Software Development and Intelligent Applications
 
Description: This course examines the dual role of artificial intelligence in modern software development: as a transformative tool for developer productivity and as a core architectural component of next-generation software. Students will master AI-assisted development workflows to optimize the entire software development life cycle, leveraging intelligent tools for requirements analysis, code generation, debugging, and automated testing. The course provides rigorous, hands-on experience in full-stack development, teaching students how to architect and integrate large language models (LLMs) and AI agents into scalable applications. By utilizing industry-standard tools for version control, CI/CD, and cloud deployment, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of building, managing, and maintaining AI-native software at every stage of its life cycle.
 
Pre-Reqs: CS400 or concurrent enrollment in CS 400
 
Required for course: Claude Code subscription

description: Theory and algorithms for nonlinear optimization, focusing on unconstrained optimization. Line-search and trust-region methods; quasi-Newton methods; conjugate-gradient and limited-memory methods for large-scale problems; derivative-free optimization; algorithms for least-squares problems and nonlinear equations; gradient projection algorithms for bound-constrained problems; and simple penalty methods for nonlinearly constrained optimization. Students are strongly encouraged to have knowledge of linear algebra and familiarity with basic mathematical analysis.

title: Adv Topics in Reinforc Lrning
description: Topics selected from advanced areas.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Topic Title:  Advanced Topics in Reinforcement Learning

Breadth Band/Area:  Band 4

Description:  Reinforcement learning is the branch of machine learning that studies how an agent can learn from taking actions and receiving feedback in an unknown environment. In the past decade, reinforcement learning algorithms have demonstrated impressive empirical successes ranging from beating a human world champion at the board game Go to allowing robots to learn difficult manipulation skills. This course aims to introduce students to reinforcement learning and topics at the forefront of reinforcement learning research. The first half of the course provides an introduction to RL fundamentals and then covers advanced topics in the reinforcement learning research literature such as hierarchical and deep reinforcement learning. The course will assume familiarity with probability, statistics, and topics covered in an introductory machine learning class. Familiarity with the Python programming language is recommended.

Strong Backgrounds / Prerequisites:  None but the course will assume familiarity with probability, statistics, linear algebra, and topics covered in an introductory machine learning class (linear regression, neural networks, etc). Familiarity with the Python programming language is recommended.

title: AI Agents for Science
description: Topics selected from advanced areas.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Topic Title: AI Agents for Science

Band/Area: Band 4

Description: AI agents are changing the way we interact with computational devices and have the potential to revolutionize how we do science: rather than a single prompt and a response, an agent can plan, use tools, reflect on intermediate results, and collaborate with human users and other agents. This course will explore the foundations and practice of building these powerful agents for scientific discovery. We will study the key ingredients behind modern agents: planning, memory, tool use, verification, and coordination, as well as how these interact with models and systems. Our focus will be on studying and developing agents that can read papers, generate and test hypotheses, run analyses, design experiments, coordinate scientific workflows, and produce reproducible research work. Familiarity with machine learning is assumed

Strong background: Solid familiarity with machine learning

description: Topics selected from advanced areas.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Topic Title:  Systems Verification

Course Website:  https://tchajed.github.io/sys-verif-fa26

Breadth Band/Area:  Band I

Description:  This is a graduate-level class on systems verification: how to mathematically prove the correctness of programs with machine-checked proofs. A core technique throughout the class is separation logic, which we will use to reason about real-world programs written in Go, including using loop invariants, reasoning about slices, pointer-based data structures, and concurrency. Programming assignments will involve proving theorems with the Rocq prover.

Strong Backgrounds / Prerequisites:  The two main requirements are "mathematical maturity" and "programming experience." Mathematical maturity means you're comfortable with being precise and learning new math, which is required to understand program proofs. No prior experience with Rocq is required.

title: Quantum Algorithms
description: Advanced topics in algorithms, complexity, and cryptography. The exact topic varies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Topic Title:  Quantum Algorithms
 
Description:  This course focuses on the algorithmic aspects of quantum computing. We develop a quantum model of computation, and discuss paradigms of efficient quantum computation, including amplitude amplification, phase estimation, quantum walks, and quantum signal processing. We apply the paradigms to computational problems such as satisfiability, the hidden subgroup problem (including integer factoring and discrete log), simulation, and solving systems of linear equations.
 
Band 3
 
Strong Backgrounds / Prerequisites:  No strict prerequisites but strong background suggested in Linear algebra (eigenvalues and eigenvectors) at the level of Math 341, probability theory at the level of Math 431, and theoretical computer science at the level of CS 577 or CS 520.

description: Develop an understanding of immigrant health in the United States from the perspective of social and structural determinants. title: Best Practices in Community-Engaged Scholarship
description: Community-engaged scholarship (CES) captures a broad understanding of the possibilities to learn, teach, and do research through academic-community collaboration. CES encompasses the interaction known as "service-learning" or "community-based learning" (CBL) as well as complex models of academic-community engagement known as "community-based research" or "participatory action research." Staff members from the Morgridge Center for Public Service (MCPS) will introduce the concepts and models of CES, discuss the importance of building and maintaining community relationships, identify challenges and solutions in implementing CES, and assist you in creating your own course, project, or proposal.

title: Social and Cultural Foundations of Counseling
description: Review of theory and research into social identity and cultural foundations of counseling including: (a) the societal context for bias, discrimination and differential treatment of sociocultural groups including but not limited to diversity of sexual orientation, gender expression, social class, cultural/ethnic/racial groups, ability status among other groups; (b) human diversity in social norms, cultural values, social identities, as well as intergroup and intragroup relations; (c) counselors' roles in developing cultural competence, reducing bias and discriminatory treatment of subgroups, and advocating for social justice; and (d) the practice implications of for providing cultural competence in serving across forms of sociocultural diversity.

input: Social and Cultural Foundations of Counseling

description: Political, historical, and cultural analysis of Chicanx/e, Mexican American, and Latinx/e students' experiences in K-12 education in the United States. title: Incarceration and Education
description: Investigates how the systems of incarceration and education operate alongside, within, around and through one another. Provides a historical examination of how education and incarceration have interacted. Presents firsthand accounts of those who work and live in the carceral system currently.
