description: Covers the major issues in international relations since the end of World War II including: the causes of war; civil wars and ethnic conflict; economic development; international trade; exchange rates and international monetary relations; international capital flows and financial crises; foreign direct investment; globalization and the environment; the UN, the IMF, World Bank, WTO, and other international organizations; and international law and human rights. title: Introduction to Comparative Politics (Honors)
description: Introduction to Comparative Politics, one of the four sub-fields in Political Science, which involves the comparative analysis of political institutions, processes, and outcomes at the national level. Examines how to usefully compare politics in a variety of countries and makes comparisons explicit and systematic in order to determine how governments work, how power is organized and contested at the national level, and how people can participate and pursue their interests in different political settings. Includes key concepts, theories, methods, and country case studies.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This course is an introduction to some of the key concepts and theoretical approaches in the comparative politics subfield of political science, and to politics in select countries. Comparative politics is the study of politics within countries (whereas international relations is the study of interactions between countries). Prompted by real-world events and puzzles, comparativists investigate broad theoretical questions such as: How and why do countries democratize (or not)? What are different ways that states organize politics, i.e., how do they differ in terms of party systems, electoral rules, presidential powers, etc.? What is the relationship between the economy and the political system?

We will spend about half of the semester focusing on key concepts in comparative politics, and the final half studying those concepts in a sample of countries. The seven countries that we will study in depth are the United Kingdom, India, Mexico, South Africa, Ukraine, Iran, and China. These represent many regions of the world and range from authoritarian regimes to newly democratic states and long-established democracies. The overall objective of the course is to give students grounding in the basic tools of comparative political analysis so that you can better understand world events and politics in countries around the world.

title: Law, Politics and Society
description: Introduction to the legal process. Examination of the various concepts of law, the perennial problems of the law, legal reasoning, and the nature and function of law and the courts.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course is designed to provide students with an introduction to the American legal system.  We begin by exploring the sources of law, examining how legal norms emerge from each of our branches of government and what happens when these norms clash.  We then turn to the key institutional components of our legal system, focusing on the structure of the US court system and the players within it.  We will compare the federal and state courts, looking at the differences in how judges are selected and how cases proceed through the system.  We will pay particular attention to the inherent conflict between the desire for independence and accountability within our judiciary and will assess how well we have done in balancing these goals.  We will also look at the alternatives to courts and investigate why they emerged and how they are currently being used.  We will put all of this knowledge to use by studying the disputing process in the civil (non-criminal) context.  We will start by developing a framework for how disputes evolve and what tends to encourage and/or discourage people from pursuing grievances.  After Thanksgiving, we will explore two case studies of civil disputes.  The first is one of the most well-known "test  cases, namely the case that culminated with the landmark Supreme Court decision in Brown v. Board of Education that ended segregation based on race in US public schools (at least on paper).  The second is the class action dispute memorialized in the bestseller, A Civil Action.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
Part 1: Sources of Law (includes classes on legal culture, judicial opinions, judicial review, legislation, regulations)
Part 2: Key Components of the US Legal System (includes classes on state courts, federal courts, judicial selection, judicial accountability, lawyers, alternative dispute resolution) 
Part 3: Understanding the Disputing Process (includes classes on the structure of disputes, the alleged litigation explosion, formal constraints on disputing)
Part 4: Constructing Disputes (includes classes on actual cases and how they evolved)

This course will examine the many factors that affect voter participation and how voters
make decisions. Together we will explore theories dealing with party identification,
group and geographic patterns, economic accountability, issue voting, and more. A
nagging question will be present throughout all of these topics: do American elections
facilitate making "good  decisions?

Specific learning outcomes for this course are to: (1) develop a theoretical and empirical
understanding of how individuals make voting decisions, (2) be able to analyze factors
that affect the results of particular elections, (3) interpret surveys and election data to
analyze how specific variables affect voters, and (4) develop a basis for evaluating the
health of the U.S. electoral system.

title: United States Congress
description: Principles, procedures and problems of the legislative process of the United States Congress. Not open to students with credit for POLI SCI 426

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The US Constitution created three branches of government -- legislative, executive and judicial--and an elaborate system of checks and balances to divide power between them. This class focuses on the legislative branch to explore: How does Congress work? How are laws really made today? How can Congress serve as a check on presidential and judicial power? How do those branches check Congress? What motivates members of Congress? We're going to answer those questions and explore the steps of the legislative process through a semester long simulation in which each student will take on the role of one Democratic member and one Republican member. This course involves active participation, learning by doing, and perspective-taking (of Members of Congress, of Republicans, and of Democrats). Instead of a few high-stress major assignments, this course involves frequent small assignments to build knowledge throughout the semester.

instructorProvidedContent.format:
This four-credit course meets for two-75 minute lectures and one 50-minute section.  We'll learn about and experience the steps of the legislative process through a semester long simulation in which each student will take on the role of one Democratic member and one Republican member. This course involves active participation, learning by doing, and perspective-taking (of Members of Congress, of Republicans, and of Democrats). Instead of a few high-stress major assignments, this course involves frequent small assignments to build knowledge throughout the semester.

Each week across lecture and section, we'll incorporate two simulation activities. These involve everything from learning about your legislator's background and constituents, to drafting bills, designing an advertising strategy for election, recording a short campaign commercial, committee hearings and markup sessions, and finally debating and voting on your legislation.

title: The Civil-Military Paradox in U.S. Politics and Society
description: Protecting a democratic nation from foreign threats often requires that nation to create a powerful military. Yet the creation of a powerful military may undermine the democracy that it is designed to protect. How do, and how should, democracies manage the paradoxical relationship between civilian authority and military institutions. Explores civilian and military perspectives in U.S. civil-military relations; address issues such as the use of military advice by civilian leaders, military challenges to civil authority, and tensions generated by shared responsibility for national security between the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. Studies how civil-military relations impact wider American society by examining the garrison state hypothesis; debates centered upon the draft versus an all-volunteer force; issues of equity and inclusion; and current concerns regarding a civil-military "gap."

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Protecting a democratic nation from foreign threats often requires that nation to create a powerful military.  Yet the creation of a powerful military may undermine the democracy that it is designed to protect.  How do, and how should, democracies manage the paradoxical relationship between civilian authority and military institutions?  By exploring civilian and military perspectives, this course addresses issues in U.S. civil-military relations such as the use of military advice by civilian leaders, military challenges to civil authority, and tensions generated by shared responsibility for national security between the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. 

The course also explores how civil-military relations impact wider American society by examining debates centered upon the draft versus an all-volunteer force; controversies regarding a potential civil-military "gap," politicization of the military, issues of equity and inclusion; and other critical questions.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
WEEKS 1-5. UNIT ONE: CMR FUNDAMENTALS introduces the essential language, concepts, and debates shaping civil-military relations, past and present. This unit concludes by examining how and why the founding documents (the Constitution and Declaration of Independence) frame the nation's civil-military dialog and practices. 

WEEKS 5-7. UNIT TWO: THE MILITARY AND THE PEOPLE addresses how military institutions and culture interact with wider U.S. society. This unit includes an examination of equity and inclusion issues, as they apply to military service. 

WEEKS 8-10. UNIT THREE: THE MILITARY AND THE GOVERNMENT examines how civil-military considerations shape and are shaped by U.S. politics, policy, and strategy. We consider military-government interactions within both international and domestic contexts.. 

WEEKS 11-13. UNIT FOUR: RECONCILING THE PARADOX explores the major theoretical traditions informing the study of civil-military relations, starting with the pioneering groundwork of Samuel Huntington and Morris Janowitz and concluding with current perspectives.

WEEKS 14-15. THE CAPSTONE EXERCISE offers a culminating experience for the course with a dynamic, turn-based simulation modeling how democratic civil-military relations function in the real-world. Together with your classmates, you will actualize all the course learning objectives by applying CMR knowledge and concepts to address a variety of political and social issues.
instructorProvidedContent.format:
Learning in PS 338 centers on the in-person classroom experience. Regular attendance and active engagement in class account for a significant share of the final grade. While these is some flexibility on attendance, students who miss class frequently typically struggle to succeed in the course, regardless of performance on exams or written assignments.

PS 338 class sessions feature a blended, active-learning format. A typical class period may include a 20-40 minute mini-lecture delivered by the instructor, integrated with various student learning activities. Classroom learning activities may include polls or surveys, short in-class writing assignments, group discussions, or other each designed to help clarify, interact with, and apply key ideas and concepts introduced in the course readings and lectures and perhaps have some fun in the process! Such activities may be structured for individual or group work, as determined by the instructor.      

Preparation for the class sessions normally includes reading and/or media assignments, along with journal entries reflecting based on the readings, etc.  

Graded assignments for the course include the regular reading journal entries, classroom learning activities, a scaffolded research project (culminating in a 4-5 page issue brief), and periodic quizzes covering key concepts presented in the course.

title: State-Building: How States Are Formed, Function, and Influence Society
description: Exploration of state-building: examining how states are formed, how they develop and maintain political power, and the ways in which they shape society. Draw on insights from political science, but also economics, history, and anthropology, to learn about the processes of state formation, the importance of state capacity, and the state's role in war, governance, and social justice. Topics will include the relationship between the state and issues like the environment, gender, and identity, highlighting both the challenges and opportunities states face in a rapidly changing world. Analysis of historical and contemporary examples from various political systems yields insights into the state's role as both a force for order and a driver of social change. Lectures, discussions, and case studies, will lead to a deeper understanding of the state's central role in global politics and everyday life.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Why do some governments build roads and schools while others collapse into chaos? How did the modern state become the most powerful institution on the planet? And why does the state sometimes fail the people it's supposed to serve?
This course explores how states are built, how they wield power, and how they shape everything from war and justice to gender, identity, and the environment. We'll draw on political science, economics, history, and anthropology to tackle big questions: Why are some states strong and others fragile? What makes governments capable or corrupt? And what happens when states try to control societies that resist them?
Through lectures, discussions, and real-world case studies from state-building experiments in Africa and the Middle East to the origins of bureaucracy in the United States you'll develop tools to analyze the state as both a force for order and a driver of change. You'll come away with a sharper understanding of the institution that, for better or worse, shapes nearly every aspect of global politics and daily life.

Feel free to reach out to me with questions about the course or a draft syllabus (sjhenn@wisc.edu)

title: Global Access to Justice
description: Lawyers are present in all countries, but their roles vary tremendously. In some countries, lawyers are greatly respected and are seen as making an important contribution by representing their clients and participating in the political process. In other countries, lawyers are viewed as less essential, perhaps even as a nuisance. Study lawyers in many different countries in an effort to explain the variation in their status and the consequent impact on citizens' access to justice.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Almost every country has lawyers, but their roles vary tremendously. In some countries, lawyers are greatly respected and are seen as making an important contribution by representing their clients and participating in the political process. In other countries, lawyers are viewed as less essential, perhaps even as a nuisance. We will explore the reasons for these variations, looking at the impact of history and the political system. We will study lawyers in many different countries in an effort to explain the variation in their status.

Our exploration of the variations in the role of lawyers will begin with legal education. We will compare the U.S. system, which requires prospective lawyers to persevere through a 3-year graduate program, with the rest of the world, where law is mostly an undergraduate enterprise.  We will then study the differences in the organization of the legal profession and will explore the relationship between its institutional structure and its legitimacy. Once again, we will find that the U.S. is an outlier, with its unified legal profession, in which all those who hold themselves out as lawyers must pass a bar exam. In most of Europe and Latin America, graduates of law programs tend to identify in terms of their specialties, e.g., as a litigator, prosecutor, or judge, rather than as a generic lawyer. 

We will also study the relationship between clients and lawyers, paying attention to the different ways in which lawyers seek out clients, how lawyers are compensated, and what happens to clients who lack the resources to hire lawyers. We will find that many countries (though not the U.S.) are open to individuals with some training, but without a law degree, providing advice to citizens under certain circumstances.

Readings for the class will include memoirs of practicing lawyers from different countries, novels and short stories about lawyers, social science research on the legal profession, and statistics about the legal profession. Readings will encompass the experiences of many different countries, but with an emphasis on lawyers in the U.S., the U.K., Germany, Russia, and China.

Week 2: The organization of the legal profession (bar associations)
Week 3: Comparing the roles of lawyers in democratic and authoritarian regimes
Week 4: Legal education
Week 5: Who tends to be left out (race, ethnicity, gender)
Week 6: Criminal defense lawyers
Week 7: Prosecutors
Week 8: Lawyers at law firms (corporate law practice)
Week 9: "In house" lawyers (working for companies)
Week 10: Lawyers in politically charged cases (cause lawyering)
Week 11: Public interest lawyering
Weeks 12-15: Lawyer-client relationships -- case studies

title: International Political Economy
description: Analyzes the interaction of politics and economics in the international arena, both historically and in the contemporary era of globalization. Focuses on international trade, monetary, and financial relations in both developed and developing economies. Not open to students with credit for POLI SCI 371 prior to fall 2017

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course examines the politics of international economic relations and economic policy. It focuses on the ways in which domestic and international politics affect both national economic policymaking and developments in the world economy. The course begins with a discussion of the analytical "building blocks  of international political economy, which we can use to understand and explain the causes and effects of trends in the world economy. It then examines the rise, fall, and return of "globalization  -- high levels of trade, monetary, and financial integration in the international economy -- over the last 150 years. Our goal will be not only to describe this historical evolution of the world economy, but also to explain its causes and consequences. Finally, the course examines a variety of key issues in the contemporary global economy. These topics include: trade policy; international financial institutions; development and industrial policy; global value chain; economic statecraft; climate change; and the rise of China. Prerequisites: PS 140 (or IS 101) and junior/senior standing; 1 course in economics is strongly recommended. If you have not fulfilled these requirements, please speak with me before enrolling in the course.

title: Machiavelli and His World
description: Introduces students to the major works of Machiavelli through the close reading of his writings in cultural and historical contexts. Discussion and targeted writing assignments will aim at cultivating in students 1) a broad understanding of Machiavelli's principal intellectual attitudes, 2) a deeper understanding of his literary sensibility, and 3) the ability to articulate controversies and complexities surrounding his thought.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
MACHIAVELLI and HIS WORLD *** This is a 300-level class, but first-year and second-year students are welcome, since no prior knowledge of Machiavelli's wrtitings is assumed.
Imperialist or pacifist? Patriot or traitor? Poet or scientist? Did you know that Machiavelli desired peace? Did you know that Machiavelli has a fantastic sense of humor? Did you know that he wrote in every literary genre -- treatise, letters, comedy, poetry, dialogue?  He is so often misunderstood! Let's find out why. This course introduces students to the major works of Machiavelli through the close reading and discussion of his writings in their cultural and historical contexts. Students will deepen their understanding of Machiavelli's thought by considering historical, literary, cultural, artistic, and political points of view.  We will aim at cultivating a deeper understanding of the controversies surrounding Machiavelli, and developing the ability to articulate the complexities of his political thought. First,  students will encounter Machiavelli's texts on their own, with guidance from lectures. Students will have the opportunity to react to Machiavelli's writing before grappling with its reception and interpretation.  Students will then deepen their understanding of Machiavelli's thought in discussion with the professor and amongst themselves. Lectures include presentation of major interpretations, but students are encouraged to think for themselves.  Discussion and targeted writing assignments will aim at cultivating in students a broad understanding of Machiavelli's principal intellectual (literary, political-theoretical, historical) attitudes.

title: Environmental Political Thought
description: Consider key paradigms of environmental thought, including political ecology, ecomodernism, ecosocialism, and ecofascism. In light of environmental degradation and crisis, investigate how these conceptual lenses offer divergent diagnoses of and prescriptions for environmental harm. Investigate the ways in which environmentally related domination and inequity may be linked to the legacies of racism, colonialism, and gender hierarchy. Analyze whether and in what way these forms of domination and inequity can be conceptualized as environmental injustices. Finally, explore different drivers of and impediments to environmental political action, ranging from environmental social movements and calls for climate justice, to climate denialism and potentially apathy-inducing phenomena like eco-anxiety.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This is a course on legal doctrine, not on policy or philosophy. That means we will
primarily focus on what the case law (i.e., judicial opinions) says, whether and how
majority opinions apply precedent, and how society may operate within the parameters
set by courts. In other words, you will learn the legal analytical structure that Courts
apply when analyzing First Amendment claims. As such, this class emphasizes case law
and analysis, as opposed to political theory and philosophy (although, I do have suggested reading that examines these aspects of free expression). We will cover the
material in a manner that focuses on the operation of the legal system as it relates to the
right to freedom of expression and the role of the lawyer, as well as the trial and
appellate judge within that system.

title: Policy-Making Process
description: Examines the political, social, and economic contexts that shape and are shaped by policy making processes. Though the focus is on the US, international comparisons will be made, and students are encouraged to think about the American context through comparative and international perspectives. Familiarizes students with dominant theories and models of policymaking process and policy change, starting with the model of the policy cycle. Focuses in on key topics and issues in policy making, specifically, agenda setting, implementation, and the relationships between policymaking and democracy. Reflects on contemporary and emerging issues and dilemmas of the politics of policy making.

title: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in Latin American society and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Brazil has long inspired curiosity in intellectual and artistic outsiders: from Michel de Montaigne's inauguration of the modern essay ("Of Cannibals,  1580) to Claude Levi-Strauss' notorious "writing lessons  in Tristes Tropiques (1955) to Michel Foucault's emergent theories of power in the 1970s and into Global Black studies of the 21st century. This interdisciplinary graduate seminar analyzes how Brazil   the place as well as the idea; the former colony and nation-state, as well as its representations   generates theory. Encounters and clashes among strikingly different peoples and worldviews shape how intellectuals and artists, both foreign and national, understand Brazil. Its staggering heterogeneity -- from pre-conquest cosmologies and especially beginning with the profoundly unequal European-Indigenous-African contact zones in the 15th and 16th centuries   makes it a singular incubator to understand theory as an inquiry into how knowledge grapples with what is new, unfamiliar, or unthinkable to it, as a perpetual search for knowledge in modernity, in worlds of mixture, conflict, and difference. The frequent motif of Brazil as a puzzle to both foreigners and Brazilians alike is perhaps best captured in political theorist Francisco de Oliveira's (2003) memorable metaphor of the duckbilled platypus, a walking paradox: at once reptile, bird, mammal - all three or none of these. In this course, we will trace how a Brazil imagined   "in theory,  in our everyday language, means an untested hypothesis   is also a story about what theory is and does. We will read theoretical essays by Brazilian and international thinkers and analyze works of the visual and literary arts from Brazil as aesthetic theory. The course will be of special interest to students of postcolonial or decolonial thought and Latin American/Caribbean studies. No knowledge of Brazil or Latin America is required. Students with reading knowledge of Portuguese will be encouraged to read in the original language.

title: Conspiracies in Public Health
description: Skepticism and conspiracism can be barriers to successful implementation of public health and medical interventions such as vaccination, fluoridation of water, and HIV treatment. Conversations between people with opposing viewpoints, whether face-to- face or via social media, often devolve to disparagement and dismissal. Awareness of or experience with such exchanges causes us to avoid tackling such "hot button" topics with friends, colleagues, and members of our communities. While it is all too easy to believe people who adopt conspiracy theories to be members of the fringe, research has shown that medical conspiracy theories are widely known, broadly endorsed, and highly predictive of many common health behaviors. Prepares health professionals to educate communities about important public health and medical interventions.

description: Examines the intersection of human, animal, and environmental health within the context of the Anthropocene. Drawing on the One Health framework, explore how globalization, ecological change, and human activity contribute to health disparities, the emergence of infectious diseases, and shifts in global public health priorities. Explore the epidemiology of infectious diseases, health determinants across diverse populations, and the ecological, social, and economic factors that facilitate disease transmission and emergence. title: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in Latin American society and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Brazil has long inspired curiosity in intellectual and artistic outsiders: from Michel de Montaigne's inauguration of the modern essay ("Of Cannibals,  1580) to Claude Levi-Strauss' notorious "writing lessons  in Tristes Tropiques (1955) to Michel Foucault's emergent theories of power in the 1970s and into Global Black studies of the 21st century. This interdisciplinary graduate seminar analyzes how Brazil   the place as well as the idea; the former colony and nation-state, as well as its representations   generates theory. Encounters and clashes among strikingly different peoples and worldviews shape how intellectuals and artists, both foreign and national, understand Brazil. Its staggering heterogeneity -- from pre-conquest cosmologies and especially beginning with the profoundly unequal European-Indigenous-African contact zones in the 15th and 16th centuries   makes it a singular incubator to understand theory as an inquiry into how knowledge grapples with what is new, unfamiliar, or unthinkable to it, as a perpetual search for knowledge in modernity, in worlds of mixture, conflict, and difference. The frequent motif of Brazil as a puzzle to both foreigners and Brazilians alike is perhaps best captured in political theorist Francisco de Oliveira's (2003) memorable metaphor of the duckbilled platypus, a walking paradox: at once reptile, bird, mammal - all three or none of these. In this course, we will trace how a Brazil imagined   "in theory,  in our everyday language, means an untested hypothesis   is also a story about what theory is and does. We will read theoretical essays by Brazilian and international thinkers and analyze works of the visual and literary arts from Brazil as aesthetic theory. The course will be of special interest to students of postcolonial or decolonial thought and Latin American/Caribbean studies. No knowledge of Brazil or Latin America is required. Students with reading knowledge of Portuguese will be encouraged to read in the original language.

input: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area

description: Provides a comprehensive understanding of the underpinnings of Infant, Early Childhood and Family Mental Health. Learn about pregnancy, transition to parenthood and typical/atypical development and attachment relationships. Become familiar with reliable and valid screening and assessment tools of social, emotional, cognitive, communication, motor and regulatory capacities in infants and young children in the context of their caregiving relationships;  developmentally appropriate diagnostic nosologies; methods of conceptualizing risk and protective factors; and planning for therapeutic interventions that build on strengths and address vulnerabilities. Unique features include assessment of early parent-child relationships and the use of video replay to engage parents in assessing their relationship with their child and the benefit of faculty from multiple departments at UW and luminary national guest instructors.

title: Seminar in Reflective Practices and Mindfulness in Infant, Early Childhood & Family Mental Health I
description: Provides a foundation in reflective practices through discussion of cases, infant and family observations and mindfulness experiences as applied to work with infants, young children and families. Explore and experience ways in which reflective practices may be applied to parent-infant/early childhood mental health. Learn mindfulness strategies for developing self-awareness and regulation that may be brought to their work with families of infants and young children. Experience both descriptive and in-vivo examples of reflective practice through case based presentations, deeper introspection and supportive discussion to increase clarity and engagement in work with families of young children. Consider boundaries and ethical decision making related to the dilemmas faced by professionals working with families during the perinatal period and in early childhood, especially those in high risk and challenging circumstances.

title: Sports Psychiatry: Improving the Mental Health of Athletes at the Individual and Systems Levels
description: Improve skills in providing psychiatric health care to athlete populations. Sports psychiatry as a sub-specialty within psychiatry focuses on diagnosis and treatment of psychiatric illness in athletes. While utilization of psychological approaches to enhance performance can be part of the work of the sports psychiatrist, the emphasis is more on addressing actual mental illness in this population. Sports psychiatry may also involve the use of exercise as a therapeutic or preventative intervention for mental illness. Sports psychiatry typically focuses on mental health care for individual athletes, but systems-wide initiatives (e.g., at the level of the team or university) are also often important.

input: Sports Psychiatry: Improving the Mental Health of Athletes at the Individual and Systems Levels

description: Introduction to common psychiatric diagnoses (mood disorders, psychotic disorders and personality disorders) in the hospital setting. title: Psychiatry Assessment & Treatment in a Forensic Hospital Setting
description: Interact with and learn from multiple staff at Mendota Mental Health Institute (MMHI), including forensic psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses, and occupational therapists. Interact with patients who have been committed to MMHI usually for forensic purposes- the patient has been found not guilty by reason of insanity, they are incompetent to stand trial, and/or their conditional release in the community has been revoked. Opportunity to see patients who have been civilly committed. Rotate with multiple psychiatrists, some of whom are specially trained in forensic psychiatry. Learn more about the forensic/legal system, the structure of medium and maximum security forensic psychiatry units, treatment of refractory psychotic and mood disorders, and the basics of forensic assessments. The student is given as much autonomy as possible with individual supervision and discussion.

input: Psychiatry Assessment & Treatment in a Forensic Hospital Setting

description: Focuses on the role that psychological principles, research evidence and social science play in the laws of U.S. society, especially in the policies and mechanisms of social control of human behavior. title: Psych of Human-Animal Interact
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: In this capstone course, we will take an in-depth look at the diversity of human-animal relationships. We will examine the types of species that humans most often interact with, and why humans form bonds with some species and not others. We will also look at the specific nature of these relationships, such as how we interact differently with companion animals, wildlife, and animals in agricultural and research settings. We'll consider how we can better understand our connections with animals by examining these relationships from both human and animal perspectives. We'll also address how an understanding of communication across species can improve relationships for both sides. Finally, by investigating some hotly-debated topics (e.g., Is it ethical to eat meat? Use animals for biomedical research? Breed animals for extreme characteristics for sporting competitions?), we'll develop an appreciation for the fact that human-animal relationships are complex, and that a variety of strong opinions exist regarding many of these relationships.

description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Technology, Growth, and Change: Development in the Digital Age

This course explores not only how technology shapes human development across the lifespan but also how developmental psychology is being shaped by ever-evolving technology. From birth through late adulthood, we will examine how digital tools, social media, artificial intelligence, and more influence growth and development. Through examining materials such as experimental research and case studies, students will critically evaluate both the benefits and challenges of technology in modern development. Special attention will be given to ethical considerations, digital literacy, and the evolving relationship between humans and technology.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Gesture in Thinking, Speaking & Communicating

This course focuses on the role of the body in thinking, speaking, and communicating, with a primary focus on gestures, which are movements of the hands and body. The course will address a range of questions, including the following: Why do people move their bodies when they think or speak? What roles do gestures and other body movements play in producing and comprehending language? How do people adapt their online and mediated communication to invoke body movements or to compensate for their absence? What roles do gestures and other body movements play in teaching and learning? Are there individual, developmental, or cultural variations in how people use body movements in speaking and thinking? The course will be discussion format, with most readings drawn from primary sources. Over the course of the semester, students will design and carry out a small-scale, original project on a relevant topic of interest, either independently or as part of a team.

title: Neuropsychology & Development
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Course description: Within this cognitive psychology class, students will become familiar with research and theories that look to explain human thought and behavior from two seemingly disparate vantage points, developmental psychology and neuropsychology. Although these two disciplines are motivated by similar questions regarding how humans acquire, maintain and use knowledge to engage with the world, potentially informative connections between the two scientific disciplines are often not brought to light. This class will juxtapose studies across the developmental life span from infancy to adulthood with patients diagnosed with a neuropsychological impairment so that students can better consider the possibilities of converging evidence or marked and informative differences between the research cohorts.

title: Gender Development
description: Special topics in Psychology at the advanced undergraduate level. May be repeated for credit with different titles.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How do we come to understand our gendered selves? Why does gender emerge as a central social category in early childhood? In this seminar we will explore children's reasoning about gender through a social cognitive development lens. We will cover empirical literature and supplemental text on children's gender development spanning from infancy to adolescence. We will examine traditional and contemporary theories of gender development from the 1950s to the present day. Topics include infant face processing, constancy and stability, categorization, social preferences, essentialism, stereotyping, gender nonconformity, androgyny, and transgender and gender diverse identities. We will explore themes of continuity and discontinuity across development, cultures, and identities. Students will be assessed via seminar participation, discussion leading, discussion board posting, 2 short papers, and a final presentation.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How does trauma affect the mind and body? Why do some people develop posttraumatic stress while others show resilience? In this course, students will learn about key concepts such as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), developmental differences in trauma responses, and factors that influence risk and resilience. Emphasis will be placed on theoretical frameworks, assessment and diagnosis, and evidence-based, strength-focused approaches to treatment. Course activities include brief lectures, discussions, student-led presentations, and applied reflection to connect research with real-world contexts.

title: Contemporary Public Policy Issues
description: Offers a general primer on large-scale policies directed by US federal and state governments, with specific examples in pressing policy areas. Takes existing policies and the policy process as a given, explains them in detail, and puts a policy focus on very specific contemporary questions of concern to policymakers. Gain a broad overall knowledge of how the majority of state and federal funding is spent and the policy outcomes associated with that spending.

footnotes:

title: Introduction to Health Policy in the United States
description: Offers an introduction to health policy in the United States. Examines the ways in which government plays a role in the provision and regulation of health care. Explores key aspects of health policy including the economics of health care (e.g., paying for and access to health care; the health care workforce; the role of markets and consequences of market/government failures, public policy that supports or promotes health; health care outcomes, quality, and disparities; and tools for evaluation) and special topics of interest such as policy addressing risky health behaviors, aging, mental health, and the Affordable Care Act. Think critically about public and private health issues using the policy analysis process, including policy interventions and their justifications, and gain skills in articulating and communicating policy positions.

input: Introduction to Health Policy in the United States

title: Advancing Public Policy in a Divided America
description: America is divided: at home, at work, and even in the media. This is true politically, as well. Given this, public policy conflict is all around us. Seek to understand and contextualize the partisan conflict present in modern American politics and policymaking today and explore individual-level tactics that public policy leaders, practitioners, and advocates may use that acknowledge conflict and attempt to move public policymaking forward. Explore ways in which policy conflict can be understood, managed, and channeled for the betterment of public policy decision-making in a divided America.

input: Advancing Public Policy in a Divided America

title: Evidence-Based Policy Making
description: Facilitates skill-building to answer questions such as how policymakers use research and evidence in their jobs, how researchers can make their work useful to policymakers, and how legislative support staff and other stakeholders use research and evidence to shape policy. Explore the definition of "evidence-based", learn about different kinds of evidence and how it is used, and learn strategies for judging the rigor of research evidence. Also explore the difference between an education-based approach to working with policymakers versus an advocacy-based approach, learn strategies for communicating research to policy makers (including written and oral presentations and data visualizations), research examples of successful evidence-based policymaking efforts, and understand the limits of using research in policymaking.

title: Discovering What Works in Health Policy
description: Introduces the key conceptual and methodological tools used in public program evaluation, with an emphasis on understanding the forces that shape health and disease as well as various policy solutions. Introduces the Potential Outcomes Framework, also known as the Rubin Causal Model. Establishes the distinction between causation from correlation using counterfactual thinking. Explores a wide variety of experimental and quasi-experimental research methods used to estimate causal effects, including randomized experiments, regression, matching, instrumental variables, fixed effects, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences, and synthetic control. Many of the causal inference methods that we discuss require statistical and computational training in order to implement. Focuses on the nontechnical conceptual, theoretical, and intuitive underpinnings of these methods that are most salient to policymakers.

input: Discovering What Works in Health Policy

Encourages active reflection on this experience and self-assessment through written assignments, reflections, and readings to help students make the most of their internships.

description: Examines the political, social, and economic contexts that shape and are shaped by policy making processes. title: Disability and the Criminal Justice System
description: Explores the interaction between the criminal justice system and disability. Explores common experiences of persons with disability such as limited access to community services, poverty, and homelessness and the connection of these experiences to mass incarceration. title: The Disability Experience
description: Introduction to the modern disability experience, with an emphasis on disability justice and advocacy.  Examines the societal implications and individual experiences of disability, centering the voices of individuals with disabilities themselves, and discusses strategies that can be used to work toward their full participation and inclusion in society.

title: Individuals with Disabilities
description: Designed to expand the knowledge base of future educators, clinicians, and society members to better understand and serve the diverse needs and interests of individuals with disabilities. Introduces the concept of disability as well as the field of special education. The history, etiology, and characteristics of specific categories of disability are examined, as are educational and other federally mandated programs designed to address the needs of both children and adults with disabilities. Topics germane to the study of disability and the field of special education are explored.

title: Positive Psychology and Well Being
description: Introduction to positive psychology, or the science of human strengths, mental health, and well-being. Positive psychology concepts are discussed within the context of health promotion, with an emphasis on minimizing the impact of illness and disability. Learn to apply positive psychology concepts in personal and professional contexts to cultivate fulfilling, healthy, and meaningful lives.

title: Disability and the Media
description: Examines the interaction between disability and media in modern society. Explore representations of disability in various forms of mass media, including television and film, social media, advertising, and others. Analyze how these representations affect disabled people directly, including the development of their identities, as well as how they influence disability attitudes and stigma throughout society. Discuss overt and casual ableism within media, as well as how the disability community uses media for activism. Discuss issues of access for disabled people (e.g., assistive technology, captions, audio descriptions), as well as the future of disability representations within media.

title: Race, Intersectionality, and Equity in Education
description: Addresses a range of issues to help teachers more thoughtfully and equitably serve their students of color and develop a critical and historical understanding of the racism, marginalization, and exclusion that is endemic to the U.S. public school system. Provides an overview of foundational constructs that  are essential for pre-service teachers preparing to teach and serve diverse students and families. Explore how race, racism, and racialization in education intersect with class, gender, dis/ability, religion, sexuality, etc. to shape inequitable schooling conditions and experiences for students of color. Analyze the effects at the individual, interactional, institutional, and societal levels Consider how power always-already enables particular policies and practices that reproduce educational inequities and hence sustain white privilege and dominance.

input: Race, Intersectionality, and Equity in Education

title: Early Childhood Special Education Methods: Inclusive Strategies for Preschool and Early Elementary
description: Covers instructional approaches and practices that support developmentally appropriate, effective, and inclusive early childhood education and evidenced-based intervention for preschool and early elementary-age children (i.e., 3-8 years old). Focuses on strategies for supporting access to the general education curriculum, participation, and achievement of young children with developmental delays and disabilities. Learn "what" to teach, the selection of developmentally- and individually-appropriate child goals and objectives, and "how" to teach, the practical components of developing and delivering effective, evidenced based instruction and intervention. Emphasis is placed on adapting general early childhood education curriculum and practices in order to support children's individualized goals within inclusive classrooms. Addresses planning and implementing instruction in alignment with state and federal mandates.

title: Development, Learning and Education Foundations in Special Education
description: Key issues and trends in special education today are examined in detail. These issues and trends are discussed within the context of ecological models of human development. Gain knowledge about child and adolescent development within the contexts of families, peer groups, schools, and communities. Apply this knowledge to teaching and practice linking these to current concepts and issues in the field. Examines the role of education and educators in providing effective supports and services to promote student learning and well-being, considering the "whole child". Gain awareness, knowledge and skills to be critical thinkers, effective educators, and leaders in the field of education including special education. Although much of what is covered will have clear implications for intervention and practice, this is not a methods or techniques course with a "how to" focus.

title: Exploring Religion in Sickness and Health
description: An introduction to the study of religion through the lens of health and health through the lens of religion employing approaches from the humanities and social sciences in conversation with health-related disciplines. It asks questions such as, How do religious peoples understand and live in sickness and health? How do people connect physical well-being to spiritual well-being? Medicine to meaning-making? How does looking at religion in sickness and health provide insight into its roles in a variety of cultures and contexts, globally and locally? How do health and religion connect particularly in situations of social marginalization and immigration? How does religion impact understandings of health and sickness beyond the borders of specific religious communities?

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
PLEASE NOTE: This is RELIG ST 102-001, lecture course with discussion sections. The HONORS-FIG RELIG ST 102 Seminar is numbered 102-002. It is open only to FIG Honors students. 
Welcome to RS 102 Exploring Religion in Sickness and Health! Yes, it's especially good preparation for students considering careers in health or health-related fields. But since everyone deals with sickness and health at some point and learning about "what matters" to people is universally important, this course is relevant for everyone. RS 102 is one of the RS "gateway" courses: That is, it's designed for students who want to learn some things about religions and religion in general and we do this via an important theme (sickness/health). 
Skills Building: comparative and interdisciplinary analysis, writing (3 short essays), religious literacy and cultural competency; conversing among multiple viewpoints
This is the gateway course for the Religious Studies certificate and major and counts toward the Global Health Certificate. It is a core course for the Health and Humanities Certificate. The course has 2 FIG sections along with 6 regular sections. You can take it for Soc Sci or HUM credit (Z).  
Course Description
How do religious peoples understand and live in sickness and health? How
does physical well-being connect to spiritual well-being? Medicine to
meaning-making? How does looking at religion in sickness and health
provide insight into its roles in different cultures and contexts? What is
"religion ? "Sickness ? "Health ? How can we understand their
relationships? From Southeast Asia to the Caribbean, Africa and the
Mediterranean, we'll approach these questions using perspectives from
anthropology, history, sociology, legal studies and the medical sciences,
among others. We'll learn how scholars of religion approach them. And
we'll be coming home to Wisconsin and the U.S. along the way to examine these
questions as well.
Course Learning Objectives
Thoughtful and prepared engagement in this class should lead you ~
--To begin to develop global religious literacy. To understand some
significant ways in which religious expressions close to home connect
to situations and cultures around the world, particularly as they relate
to sickness, health, and healing.
--To understand something of the diversity of ways in which religion
both reflects and shapes human communities and self-conceptions, as
illustrated mainly by some of the cultures influenced by Buddhism, forms of
religion with roots in Africa, and Christianity. (Other traditions are considered as well.)
--To gain knowledge of and familiarity with some approaches to  interpreting  religion and to use these to examine a variety of religious expressions related to sickness and health. We'll also test these theories against the experiences and practices of people.
--To learn and begin communicating in a vocabulary of religion and health in the humanities and social sciences and in thoughtful human discourse generally. (We'll learn a little bio-science too.)
--To gain and practice skills in analytical reading, writing and thinking about religion and particularly its connections to health. These skills are widely applicable to courses and careers outside this
class and to being a global citizen and will help you continue to learn beyond this class.

No Prerequisites; especially suitable for first and second-year students.
This is not an old-fashioned "intro to religions" course in which you
learn several "facts"  about some major religions. You will indeed do that.
But this course focuses on helping you develop ideas and skills for
understanding religion as a broad category and in specific contexts: a small
village in Thailand, an immigrant community in Appleton, a hospital room
in Chicago, a Medical School classroom in Madison. It aims to teach you
how to recognize and interpret religion and use your understanding for the
"health  of others and yourself of human communities.

title: History of Medicine in South Asia
description: Study primary and secondary sources to explore how South Asian societies have understood the ideas of health and well-being throughout history. We will consider a number of cases that illustrate uniquely South Asian conceptions of illness and physical dysfunction and the ways in which people in South Asia have attempted (and continue to attempt today) to heal bodies. Students will learn about the traditional healing systems of South Asia, including Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani, the basic components of each systems' ideas about disease pathology and treatment that have been used for centuries to heal illness, maintain good health, and, in some instances, aspire to a state of super-health that transcends the limitations of bodily existence altogether.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: How have people in South Asian societies understood and expressed ideas about health and illness, medicine and healing throughout history, in literature, and religion?  How have ideas about wellbeing and illness driven therapeutics for ailing bodies and regimens to maintain fit bodies?  Who gets to make determinations about what is fitness and unfitness and, crucially, how to shape or treat them?  These are some of the big questions that will frame our studies this semester of healing traditions, or medicines, in South Asia.  We'll read about and reflect on ways the human body is presumed to relate to disease and how people experience, carry, and convey the experience of illness.  Together we will think about how sometimes illnesses function as metaphors for social categories that people value as well as occasionally fear, and we will explore how those metaphorical expressions reveal concerns about larger cultural norms and institutions that shape the contours of our lives, such as, sex and gender, class and caste, and ethics and religion, and more.

title: Of Demons and Angels. Dante's Divine Comedy
description: Have you ever wondered about human nature? What is our place in this world? Through readings, videos, and original images, explore and discuss Dante's answers from one of the greatest world literary classics, his Divine Comedy. From Hell, through Purgatory to Paradise, we will travel together with Dante in a universal tale of the journey of the human soul. Along the way, learn about Dante, his life and his works, development of literary history, historical and socio-political context of medieval Europe, the Mediterranean and the Middle East. Make connections that cross today's geographic and cultural lines in an exploration of literary topics, the history of ideas, and shared history, pondering universal concepts and patterns in the development of civilization that can still be observed today.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
LitTrans/Medieval/Religious 253, "Of Demons and Angels. Dante's Divine Comedy in Translation"
is a 3-credit course conducted in English. 
        Satisfies humanities/literature requirement. Counts for Liberal arts and science credit in L&S intermediate.
	 It *counts* towards the Italian major and the Italian certificate.  
	 Through readings, videos, and original images, we explore the most significant episodes from one of the greatest world literary classics, Dante's Divine Comedy. From Hell, through Purgatory to Paradise, we travel together with Dante in a universal tale of the journey of the human soul. The course is based on a discussion of specific themes, characters, phenomena, that define and contextualize Dante's work. 
	 This course consists of a detailed and guided close reading and discussion of Dante's Divine Comedy. During the semester, students learn about Dante, his life and his works, development of literary history, historical and socio-political context of medieval  and early-modern Europe. Furthermore, students are invited to ponder universal concepts and patterns in the development of Western civilization that had repercussions on centuries of world history and that can still be observed today. Students make connections that cross geographic and cultural lines in an exploration of literary topics, the history of ideas, and shared history. A Canvas page has been created for this course that contains all additional materials (readings, videos, links, etc).
	 Course requirements: 3 one-hour exams (taken over the course of the semester), five quizzes, and a brief group project. No final exam.
Prerequisites: sophomore standing or consent of instructor. Honors option available.

title: God & Money
description: Explores the historical connections between capitalism and religion. Considers if and how religious ideas and practices facilitated the rise of capitalism; asks whether religious institutions have supported the reproduction of social inequalities, unjust labor practices, and exploitative economies; and studies the role played by religious actors in the critique of capitalism. Pays attention to the historical specificity of the capitalist system, its conditions of emergence in the Christian West, and the effects of its globalization on non-Christian traditions. Covers topics including classical social theories of religion and capitalism; contemporary examples of religious practice and capital accumulation; and the relationship between religious movements and social-economic justice.

title: Early Christian Literature: Matthew-Revelation
description: An exploration of Christianity's charter documents in the light of what modern scholarship has discovered about the New Testament's sociohistorical context, composition, theologies, and presentations of Jesus.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
This Fall, consider taking a course that builds transferable skills and teaches you how to continue learning beyond the course about a topic of historical, cultural and personal interest for millions of people. First-year students are welcome in this course (just email instructor for permission) as well as those with more college experience.
This course introduces the historical study of the origins of Christianity, primarily through examination of selected writings of the New Testament. It focuses on how these sources reflect what happened and what people believed and did in early Christian communities. Its first goal is acquainting students with what these sources actually say. Its second is challenging students to develop their understanding of what these sources might have meant to the first-century communities for which they were written. We will not cover every New Testament text, but we will focus on several key texts and on developing skills you can use for further study of the New Testament beyond this class.
No prior background in the academic study of the New Testament is required for this course. I recognize that students come with a range of familiarity with the New Testament and am eager to help students who may be worried about their lack of it. For everyone regardless of prior knowledge, regular preparation and active participation are the surest ways to achieve success in the course.
This course focuses on developing skills that students can use for further study in variety of fields while developing an understanding of early Christian communities and literature. It is based in conversational lectures and discussions supported with technology and a clear, engaging textbook.
Graded exercises encourage development and improvement over the course and should be low-anxiety vehicles if students prepare as instructed and participate consistently. Students with a range of career and field interests and a range of preparation have taken this course successfully. Meets LIT requirement.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:

Unit 4 covers other writings, including Revelation and 1 early Christian text that is not in the NT.

Attention to literary genres ranging from elegy to riddles; the development of Christianity; encounters with Romans, Vikings, and Normans; and other political and social concerns. All readings in translation.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Who were the people who lived in what is now England over 1000 years ago? This class explores the history, literature, religion, art, and culture of the early medieval English (c.450-c.1100). We explore a wide range of texts originally written in Latin and Old English that include fights with monsters, heartbreaking elegies, dirty riddles, bombastic sermons, and medical treatises. 

Over the semester, we will learn about how Early Medieval England came into existence, how it became Christianized, how it fought, assimilated, and fought again with Vikings, and how it all ended (or didn't!) with the Norman Conquest. As a framework for the class, we will study the literature of the period (in modern translation), but we will also explore the period's history, art, religion, architecture and everyday culture. We will also consider how Old English and Anglo-Latin literature has been adapted by modern writers, and why this early medieval culture continues to appeal to people today.

No previous experience with medieval literature and culture required!

title: Christianity in the Atlantic World, 1500-1800
description: Between the late Middle Ages and the era of democratic revolutions Western Christianity saw a series of sweeping changes that altered its global profile and helped form the modern world - examines some of these shifts and their impact. Questions explored include: Why did the Reformations of the 16th century occur and with what effects on people's lives and on early modern societies? What was the relationship between European colonization, the Atlantic slave trade, new theories of race, and the spread of Christianity to the "New World"? How was the Christian religion resisted, received, and reshaped by Native Americans and people of African descent? What sparked movements of reform and renewal - including new Catholic religious orders and the Protestant Evangelical Awakening - and with what consequences for modern Christianity? How did the nature of Christian belief and identity change under the impact of religious conflict, political revolution, and new intellectual movements?

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Between the late Middle Ages and the French Revolution (c. 1500--1800), Christianity was deeply woven into the fabric of European life, permeating politics, law, intellectual culture, and the everyday lives of ordinary people. At the same time, Western Christianity also underwent dramatic transformation. The Reformations of the sixteenth century shattered the unity of the Catholic Church based in Rome and gave rise to multiple Christian confessions.

These developments had far-reaching consequences for European and global history. Confessional divisions reshaped European politics and society and transformed how people across social classes understood and expressed their religious identities, beliefs, and practices. As Europe's colonial expansion accelerated, these religious changes also spread across the Atlantic world, profoundly affecting peoples in other parts of the globe, including those who were indigenous, or forcibly brought, to the "New World  of the Americas. This course examines these momentous shifts through key moments in the history of Christianity in the early modern Atlantic world.

title: Catastrophe Risk and Reinsurance
description: Examines market and public policy approaches for managing catastrophe risks. Describes how catastrophes such as hurricanes, wildfires, severe convective storms, terrorist attacks, cyberattacks, environmental disasters (e.g., oil spills), and epidemics create societal challenges by affecting many households and firms concurrently. Covers catastrophe models, which are used to estimate the potential losses from these events by simulating thousands of possible disaster scenarios. Describes the markets for reinsurance and insurance linked securities, how these products work, and the types of risks they cover. Compares public-private partnership models across countries for managing severe risks such as public terrorism reinsurance and cyclone risk pools to glean insights from these varying approaches.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: The starting point for this course is the images we already know of the Vikings, as seen in games like Assassins Creed: Valhalla, tv shows like "The Vikings  or even movies like Marvel's "Thor.  Where do these images come from and how are they formed in modern consciousness? Then we will look at the medieval Scandinavians themselves to learn what is known and what is not known about these people and their age. This FIG will appeal to students who are interested in learning about the present through the past and those with a specific interest in the Nordic countries. The other classes in this FIG will enhance our examination of these topics. Enrollment in an optional first-semester Swedish, Norwegian, or Danish class will enhance your understanding of the cultures of the region and is highly recommended.

title: Memory and Literature from Proust to Knausgard
description: Investigates the relations between theories of memory, both individual and collective, and modern literary representations of remembering. Survey seminal conceptions of memory in the interdisciplinary field of memory studies, investigating topics such as nostalgia, trauma, personal and cultural identity, war and Holocaust, sites of memory, and autobiographical narrative. Through the avenues opened up by these theoretical frameworks, consider the narrative forms as well as the ethical and political dimensions of remembering in major novels by Marcel Proust, W. G. Sebald, and Karl Ove Knausgard.

In this course, we will discuss topics such as nostalgia, trauma, identity, war and Holocaust, sites of memory, and autobiographical narrative. We consider these dimensions of remembering in five excellent novels from the twenty-first century.

See books for fall 2026 under textbooks.

title: History of Scandinavia to 1815
description: Political, social, economic, and cultural developments of Scandinavia through the "Viking Age" to the break-up of Sweden-Finland and Denmark-Norway; emphasis on the interplay between social and political forces and institutions and the area's relationship with the rest of Europe.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Myths and images of Vikings are everywhere, but what was really going on in Scandinavia during the Viking Age (793-1066)? And what happened in the Nordic countries between the Viking Age and the nineteenth century? This course surveys Scandinavian history all the way up to 1815. You will learn not only about medieval Scandinavia and the founding of the Scandinavian Kingdoms, but also about the fascinating changes in Northern Europe during the Reformation, the Age of the Scandinavian Empires, the Enlightenment and the beginning of the move from Kingdoms to Nations.

Important issues and concepts will include:
 	Scandinavian society in the Viking Age
 	Viking raids and settlements 
 	Political structures that changed from kinship clans to chieftainships to kingdoms
 	Religious change from Pre-Christian polytheism to the conversion to Catholicism
 	The effects of the Reformation in Scandinavia
 	Early Modern Scandinavian power struggles and the Age of Empires and Colonies
 	The Age of Enlightenment in Northern Europe
 	The loss of Empires and the move towards Nation States.

There are no prerequisites for this course other than sophomore standing and an interest in the region. You do not need to know anything about Scandinavia or have any language skills to take this course, although prior knowledge of Scandinavia and general familiarity with European history will of course be useful.

description: What constitutes heroism in the absence of universally shared moral frameworks? Who are we as individuals? topics.longDescription: Language and Worldview: Language, Culture, Mind

title: Language and Worldview
description: Writing and discussion intensive seminar that introduces students to one or more Slavic (Russian, Polish, Serbian, Czech, Croatian, Bosnian) languages, literatures, and/or cultures within a global context.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Do languages shape the way we think? For bicultural individuals, the answer to this question is obviously yes. Even, however, for students who have attained an intermediate- or advanced-level proficiency in another language, the idea that languages present different "pictures of the world  -- that language and worldview often go hand-in-hand -- seems self-evident. Indeed, questions of cross-linguistic differences about the meanings of words and concepts (does French s'amuser bien have the same meaning as English to have fun?) could be said to represent more clear-cut and stark cases of similar questions of meaning within one language (is my idea of fun really the same as yours?). Language does, in a very real way, represent a certain "picture of the world . If differences in how languages convey meaning exist, then it should certainly be possible to develop a framework for reflecting on these "linguistic pictures of the world . This course represents both an introduction to semantic analysis (how do languages encode meaning?) as well as a content-based course in comparative ethnosemantics (to what extent does language shape the way we think and how can we systematically investigate this question?). Cross-linguistic case studies of the meanings of terms and concepts -- everyday words like home, modes of conveying spatial orientation, words relating to human psychology -- will serve as practical vehicles for an explanation and a discussion of the theory of a cultural approach to semantics. In addition to this, evidence for the encoding of culture in grammatical constructions and in discourse will be introduced. We will also examine the consequences of a cultural approach to language for reading and interpreting literature. This course requires no formal background in linguistics. The course lies at the intersection of humanities proper and social sciences. One of its primary goals is to hone critical-thinking skills related to language and culture that should prove relevant to any number of academic disciplines (literature, psychology, history, political science, philosophy, anthropology, sociology, communications, education, human geography) as well as to everyday self-understanding. Please note: this is an Honors-level course.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: We'll be using textbooks and articles on cultural linguistics to gain insights into how language frames meaning. This is true within one language but particularly evident cross-linguistically, and our focus will be on the latter. Topics that we'll discuss include: color terms across languages; how spatial orientation (and "right" and "left") are represented across languages; emotion terms; cross-linguistic differences in certain grammatical constructions. We'll be doing some hands-on work with an online linguistic corpus to investigate how certain linguistic conceptualizations unfold with regard to certain key cultural words. At the end of the course, we'll also have guest speakers from various languages taught in the Department of German, Nordic, and Slavic give us insight into some word/concept or grammatical construction of interest from their particular language (or languaculture). Data will be drawn in particular from various Slavic languages (Russian, Polish, Czech, Ukrainian), but no prior knowledge of these languages is required, and we will be using these languages to exemplify general linguistic processes.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This is a community-based learning course in which students are required to complete 25 hours of volunteer work with older adults throughout the semester (approximately 2-3 hours/week). The course instructor and teaching assistant help to connect you with local agencies such as senior centers, adult day programs, and nursing facilities for this volunteer work. The classroom portion of the course connects to and complements the volunteer work.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: We cover topics such as ageism, physical changes that often come with aging, housing, transportation, isolation/loneliness, technology, caregiving, substance use, and sexuality/intimacy in later life.
instructorProvidedContent.format: The classroom portion of the class is interactive and experiential. There is a mix of small and large group discussions, activities, case examples, videos, and guest speakers. There are a maximum of 25 students in the class.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course explores topics of reproductive health, rights, and justice in the United States and across the globe. title: God & Money
description: Explores the historical connections between capitalism and religion. Considers if and how religious ideas and practices facilitated the rise of capitalism; asks whether religious institutions have supported the reproduction of social inequalities, unjust labor practices, and exploitative economies; and studies the role played by religious actors in the critique of capitalism. Pays attention to the historical specificity of the capitalist system, its conditions of emergence in the Christian West, and the effects of its globalization on non-Christian traditions. Covers topics including classical social theories of religion and capitalism; contemporary examples of religious practice and capital accumulation; and the relationship between religious movements and social-economic justice.

title: Law, Sexuality, & Society
description: Examines the legal and social development and implications of laws governing sexual behavior, human reproduction, media, privacy, and topics related to sexuality, sex and gender. Includes historical analyses of laws connected to present day regulations of sexuality, demonstrating the origins of many of the world's most frequently debated civil rights issues. Chief focus on the United States legal system, with some content including examinations of institutions around the world. Investigates taken-for-granted knowledge and assumptions about sexuality and look at legal, cultural and social constructions of sex in society. Covers intersectional social implications, including race, (dis)ability, class, etc. Topics include: obscenity, pornography, sex work, sexual surrogacy, birth control, abortion, sex education, sexual violence, sex offenders, sexual citizenship rights, trans and intersex legal topics.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This is a community-based learning course in which students are required to complete 25 hours of volunteer work with older adults throughout the semester (approximately 2-3 hours/week). title: Crime, Gender and Justice
description: Focuses on the intersection between gender, crime and justice from a cross-cultural perspective. The gendered nature of the criminal justice system, female experiences of crime, prosecution and incarceration as well as the extent to which women are victims, offenders, and participants in the criminal justice system will be explored. Special emphasis will be placed on the theoretical implications of offending behavior and the intersection of gender with sexuality, race, ethnicity and class. The goal of this course is to provide a foundation for critically assessing the often controversial issues surrounding race, gender, crime, and criminal justice in society.
