title: Antisemitism in European Culture
description: Through a critical and interdisciplinary lens, review the history and major theories of modern antisemitism in its past and present-day forms. Read scholarship on antisemitism, as well as canonical antisemitic texts, with attention to geographic, chronological, and cultural contexts. Learn about the origins, major themes, continuities and changes, and surprising endurance of antisemitism. Use historical thinking to understand antisemitism as a major historical problem and to address related contemporary issues with nuance.

title: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in Latin American society and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Brazil has long inspired curiosity in intellectual and artistic outsiders: from Michel de Montaigne's inauguration of the modern essay ("Of Cannibals,  1580) to Claude Levi-Strauss' notorious "writing lessons  in Tristes Tropiques (1955) to Michel Foucault's emergent theories of power in the 1970s and into Global Black studies of the 21st century. This interdisciplinary graduate seminar analyzes how Brazil   the place as well as the idea; the former colony and nation-state, as well as its representations   generates theory. Encounters and clashes among strikingly different peoples and worldviews shape how intellectuals and artists, both foreign and national, understand Brazil. Its staggering heterogeneity -- from pre-conquest cosmologies and especially beginning with the profoundly unequal European-Indigenous-African contact zones in the 15th and 16th centuries   makes it a singular incubator to understand theory as an inquiry into how knowledge grapples with what is new, unfamiliar, or unthinkable to it, as a perpetual search for knowledge in modernity, in worlds of mixture, conflict, and difference. The frequent motif of Brazil as a puzzle to both foreigners and Brazilians alike is perhaps best captured in political theorist Francisco de Oliveira's (2003) memorable metaphor of the duckbilled platypus, a walking paradox: at once reptile, bird, mammal - all three or none of these. In this course, we will trace how a Brazil imagined   "in theory,  in our everyday language, means an untested hypothesis   is also a story about what theory is and does. We will read theoretical essays by Brazilian and international thinkers and analyze works of the visual and literary arts from Brazil as aesthetic theory. The course will be of special interest to students of postcolonial or decolonial thought and Latin American/Caribbean studies. No knowledge of Brazil or Latin America is required. Students with reading knowledge of Portuguese will be encouraged to read in the original language.

input: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area

title: Race and Culture in the Americas
description: Examine how the experiences of marginalized groups in the U.S. are profoundly intertwined with hemispheric historical processes. Review the categories that emerged to conceptualize human difference as European colonizers dispossessed indigenous peoples of their lands and inaugurated the forced migration and enslavement of peoples from Africa. Focus on how race was transformed after the revolutions of independence, exploring key concepts such as the one drop rule, mestizaje, racial democracy, and color-blindness. Explore how race intersects with gender, class, and migration, as well as with slavery, anti-colonial struggles, and US expansionism. Examine common assumptions in comparisons of race relations -e.g., the idea of a more more "fluid" understanding of race in Latin American countries, versus the binary models of the U.S.

title: Spanish Phonetics
description: Practice course for improvement of pronunciation, and introduction to transcription and phonetic and phonemic analysis.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Spanish 320 is an advanced practice course that emphasizes improvement of pronunciation through a clear and concise introduction to phonetic and phonemic analysis in Spanish. We see how to produce the sounds of Spanish, their logical groupings/classifications and the way in which they change according to their phonetic environment. We also concentrate on applied pronunciation practice in the form of a variety of exercises and activities, and we are introduced to the phonetic transcription of Spanish language texts. We will explore the phonetic contrasts between English and Spanish in order to increase our awareness of their major articulatory differences and to improve our Spanish pronunciation. Summary analyses of some of the pronunciation differences across various Spanish dialects are explored as we work our way through the Spanish sound system.
IMPORTANT NOTE: Attendance is required.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: Each week we will study approximately one chapter from the textbook. Chapter content will be summarized and explained with examples and additional pertinent information. Afterwards, we will utilize various in-class practice exercises to better understand and apply the acquired knowledge. Homework is comprised primarily of the phonetic transcription of a specific text and of oral practice of said text both in class and via recordings submitted in Canvas. There are several short, written and oral quizzes throughout the course, in addition to a final comprehensive exam.
instructorProvidedContent.format: Small class with intensive class participation. Written and oral exams. Written homework. Textbook and some additional readings.

title: Literature of the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries
description: Historical survey of the literature of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Major authors and representative works in all genres covering Neo-Classicism, Romanticism, Realism, and Naturalism. Important currents in intellectual history.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Dear Students,

This course focuses on Spanish literary texts including poetry, theater, narrative from the Neo-Classical, Romantic, Realist, and Naturalist movements of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It examines these works in relation to the political, artistic, and aesthetic contexts in which they were produced. In addition, students will have the opportunity to engage with contemporary media forms (such as graphic novels, comics, films, and video games) that reinterpret the themes and formal strategies of the texts studied, while engaging in creative, collaborative, and hands-on classroom activities. Ultimately, the course invites students to consider how past ways of thinking about life and culture can serve as valuable tools for understanding the complexities of the present and for envisioning more conscientious futures.

All materials will be available online or posted on Canvas.

I look forward to seeing you next semester!

Alicia

title: Contemporary Mayas: A Culture of Nature
description: Explore the enduring wisdom and resilience of the Maya civilization amidst historical challenges and contemporary dynamics. Delve into Maya philosophy, history, and current affairs, with a focus on their relationship with the environment. Analyze pivotal questions: Did the Maya civilization collapse or undergo intentional transformation? Why did the Maya army refrain from sacking the colonial capital during a major rebellion? Examine the impact of modern politics and economics on Maya culture. Uncover the role of Maya bioculture in cultural resistance and survival, and the interconnectedness of spirituality, health, and ethics with nature. Investigate the complexities of Maya perspectives on present-day issues.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Spanish America: Lexicon of Love
Through the genre of short story this course (all materials provided through Canvas) will explore literary representations of love in Spanish American literature of the XX and XXI centuries. We will examine how much of the ancient Greek notions of love (eros- physical love, agape- purely spiritual love, philia- love of the mind, ludus- playful love ...) remain in the repertoire of the XX and XXI century neoliberal Spanish America. Our discussions will be based on reading short stories, micro-fiction and new autofictional genres that the development on new technology-based platforms like facebook, podcasts, instagrams continue to add to the genre of short fiction. Our discussions will be framed and shaped by questioning what is codified as love in the modern globalized times and how are gender roles and expectations represented. How are masculinity and femininity defined by the patriarchal culture and in the Hispanic world? What role manhood, honor and dignity play in the construction of the concept of love? And, what is expected of women when they fall in or out of love? In addition to gender, our discussions will be mindful of race, class and social conventions. And so, we will look at lost loves, found loves, promiscuity in love and doomed love.  Works by Garc a M rquez, Jorge Luisa Borges, Julio Cort zar, Luisa Valenzuela, Ana Mar a Shua, Isabel Allende, Ana Lydia Vega and Rosario Ferr  , (among others), will provide us with examples for our discussions.  Class will be organized around discussions of the texts, short response papers and final project.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Dear Students,

In this course, we will read texts alongside images to examine how this unique combination of image and text creates and develops powerful stories about the past that shape the way we read and construct memory. First, we will study the sophisticated strategies that allow graphic novels and comics to tackle with ease topics often seen as overly sentimental, excessively controversial, or uncomfortably dark. We will see how these visual narratives use irony, humor, and a range of emotions to address themes such as the urgent need to care for the planet, the challenges of aging and losing memory, the brutality of civil war, and the tensions surrounding contemporary political issues inherited from the past. Second, we will explore how visual narrative provides fertile ground for growing fantasy worlds that confront readers with philosophical and existential questions in a palatable and engaging form, while linking past and future. Finally, we will reflect on and experiment collaboratively by creating your own comic! with the power of visual storytelling to expand our minds and promote creativity. All materials will be available online or through Canvas. 

Join us for a fun semester!!!

Alicia

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course approaches the representation of Latin American human rights issues from an interdisciplinary perspective by looking at  performances, testimonials, fiction films, documentaries as well as memory museums, monuments, photographic exhibits, advertisements and souvenirs in their accounting of human rights. The examination of collective and individual trauma will focus on the Southern Cone countries, mostly Argentina and Chile. It will pose three questions in relation to the construction of post-traumatic memory in Latin America: what is being remembered, when and how.  Course lectures and in-class discussions will look at cultural responses to human rights crisis, particularly the role of cultural forms in understanding the ethical and aesthetic approaches to accounting and representation of human rights.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
We will explore the meanings of justice and truth in these post-authoritarian societies and focus on the ways survivors, writers, visual artists, musicians, documentary and feature film makers, journalists and performance artists have tackled the issues of justice, truth, revenge, victimhood and post-traumatic memory. Our reading of culture will look into forms of social resistance, construction of memory museums, monuments, photographic exhibits, advertisements and performances in their accounting of human rights abuses. What is being remembered as well as how and when in regard to the military dictatorships in Argentina (1976-1983) and Chile (1973-1990) will shape our discussions in this course for which all the materials will be available through canvas (some visual materials such as feature films will have to be purchased through Netflix and or Amazon Prime or other venues).  We will talk about concepts of  transitional as well as poetic justice. One goal of the course is to sharpen our "critical eye and tongue  and improve each individual's skills as a reader, thinker, and writer.
Through lectures, class discussions, short essays along with video reflections we will look at cultural responses to human rights crisis, particularly the role of cultural forms in understanding the ethical and aesthetic approaches to accounting and representation of human rights.  
            This course will seek to respond to various key questions in relation to the construction of post-traumatic memory in Latin America:
 
What is being remembered, when and how?
Who has the right to remember? In what way testimonials of survivors codify themselves as a witness to crimes?
How can issues of retribution, revenge and justice, societal indifference and conformity, as well as forgiveness be articulated. Does trauma necessarily exceed any articulation?
How is the writing of those who remained in their countries under the oppressive government different from those who wrote in exile?
Can we look at the issues of memory and repression from the perspective of the memory market that has emerged with the political transitions and the accompanying neo-liberal economic projects.
How are narratives related to the issues of human rights marketed and packaged?
 Is memory market effective in transmitting the message of "never again  regarding human rights abuses? Does it resonate locally or internationally? 
What is, after all, a neo-liberal price-tag attached to the memory of the military dictatorship

 

Key words: memory, human rights, revenge, restitution, truth-telling, testimonials, justice, truth, pain of others. 

 

            We will discuss a play by Ariel Dorfman (La muerte y la doncella), listen to songs by creators of canci n de protesta chilena such as V ctor Jara, Violeta Parra, Inti Illimani, Mon Laferte, as well as see feature films La historia oficial, El secreto de sus ojos and Death and a Maiden, documentaries such as Madres de la Plaza de Mayo, see performances of outing the perpetrators such as escraches and funas, and have virtual visits to the memorials such as ESMA and Parque de la memoria en Argentina and Villa Grimaldi in Chiule, among others.
instructorProvidedContent.format: group discussions; short presentations; lectures; This course examines human rights abuses, including topics such as violence, torture, displacement, and systemic oppression. Some of the materials texts, images, and testimonies may be emotionally challenging or disturbing. Students are encouraged to engage thoughtfully and critically, while also being attentive to their own well-being.
keywords: human rights; Argentina; Chile; traumatic memory; performance; museum culture; monuments

title: Interdepartmental Seminar in the Latin-American Area
description: Interdisciplinary inquiry in Latin American society and culture.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: Brazil has long inspired curiosity in intellectual and artistic outsiders: from Michel de Montaigne's inauguration of the modern essay ("Of Cannibals,  1580) to Claude Levi-Strauss' notorious "writing lessons  in Tristes Tropiques (1955) to Michel Foucault's emergent theories of power in the 1970s and into Global Black studies of the 21st century. This interdisciplinary graduate seminar analyzes how Brazil   the place as well as the idea; the former colony and nation-state, as well as its representations   generates theory. Encounters and clashes among strikingly different peoples and worldviews shape how intellectuals and artists, both foreign and national, understand Brazil. Its staggering heterogeneity -- from pre-conquest cosmologies and especially beginning with the profoundly unequal European-Indigenous-African contact zones in the 15th and 16th centuries   makes it a singular incubator to understand theory as an inquiry into how knowledge grapples with what is new, unfamiliar, or unthinkable to it, as a perpetual search for knowledge in modernity, in worlds of mixture, conflict, and difference. The frequent motif of Brazil as a puzzle to both foreigners and Brazilians alike is perhaps best captured in political theorist Francisco de Oliveira's (2003) memorable metaphor of the duckbilled platypus, a walking paradox: at once reptile, bird, mammal - all three or none of these. In this course, we will trace how a Brazil imagined   "in theory,  in our everyday language, means an untested hypothesis   is also a story about what theory is and does. We will read theoretical essays by Brazilian and international thinkers and analyze works of the visual and literary arts from Brazil as aesthetic theory. The course will be of special interest to students of postcolonial or decolonial thought and Latin American/Caribbean studies. No knowledge of Brazil or Latin America is required. Students with reading knowledge of Portuguese will be encouraged to read in the original language.

title: Applied Categorical Data Analysis
description: "Which is more popular, Apple, PC, or Linux?" "Rate your satisfaction with this product on a scale from 1 to 5." Organizing information into categories is natural! But, canonical statistical approaches like standard linear regression are not designed for analyzing such data. Develop techniques appropriate for analyzing categorical response data, with an emphasis on their application. Topics include: multidimensional contingency tables, inference for measures of association between categorical variables, and regression modeling for categorical data - specifically, logistic & Poisson regression. Utilizes the R programming language.

title: Introduction to Deep Learning and Generative Models
description: Deep learning is a field that specializes in discovering and extracting intricate structures in large, unstructured datasets for parameterizing artificial neural networks with many layers. Since deep learning has pushed the state-of-the-art in many research and application areas, it's become indispensable for modern technology. Focuses on a understanding deep, artificial neural networks by connecting it to related concepts in statistics. Beyond covering deep learning models for predictive modeling, focus on deep generative models. Besides explanations on a mathematical and conceptual level, emphasize the practical aspects of deep learning. Open-source computing provides hands-on experience for implementing deep neural nets, working on supervised learning tasks, and applying generative models for dataset synthesis.

title: Financial Statistics
description: Today's cutting-edge quantitative trading strategies are based on complex stochastic models of financial data. Specialized statistical techniques are needed to analyze them. Study the advanced statistical methodologies now widely employed in modern finance. Topics include: discrete models such as binomial trees and GARCH; continuous models such as the Black-Scholes model; and stochastic volatility models. Emphasis will be on data analysis and statistical inference in these models, with applications to risk management. Learn about the models real quantitative traders use in their work.

title: Introduction to Stochastic Processes
description: Topics include discrete-time Markov chains, Poisson point processes, continuous-time Markov chains, and renewal processes. Applications to queueing, branching, and other models in science, engineering and business.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
Math 632 is a course on basic stochastic processes and applications with an emphasis on problem solving. Topics will include  discrete-time Markov chains, Poisson point processes, continuous-time Markov chains, and renewal processes. In class we go through theory, examples to illuminate the theory, and techniques for solving problems. Homework exercises and exam problems are paper-and-pencil calculations with examples and special cases, together with short proofs.

A typical advanced math course follows a strict theorem-proof format. 632 is not of this type. Mathematical theory is discussed in a precise fashion but only some results can be rigorously proved in class. This is a consequence of time limitations and the desire to leave measure theory outside the scope of this course. Interested students can find the proofs in the literature. For a thoroughly rigorous probability course students should sign up for the graduate probability sequence Math/Stat 733-734 which requires a background in measure theory from Math 629 or 721. An undergraduate sequel to 632 in stochastic processes is Math 635 - Introduction to Brownian motion and stochastic calculus.

The course will have two evening midterm exams, most likely around week 6 and week 10.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: As machine learning systems become increasingly widespread, there is growing demand for models whose predictions can be explained and understood by humans. This course introduces key methods and frameworks for interpretability and explainability in modern machine learning. Topics include intrinsically interpretable models such as regression and decision trees, as well as post-hoc explanation methods including feature attribution techniques like Shapley values and saliency maps. The course also examines interpretability for modern foundation models and large language models, including approaches such as probing and circuit-based analysis. Connections to causal reasoning, statistical perspectives on interpretability, feature selection and graphical models are also discussed throughout.

title: Common Anorectal Diseases
description: The diagnosis and treatment of common anorectal diseases in the context of anatomical and physiological basis as it correlates to the clinical setting. The medical and surgical treatment of anorectal disorders will be discussed from the historical background to modern management algorithms. Topics will include fissures, perirectal abscess, fistula-in-ano, external and internal hemorrhoidal diseases, pruritus ani, fecal incontinence, rectal prolapse, obstructive defecation, sexually transmitted infections, and various anorectal manifestations of irritable bowel disease. Symptomatic presentation and natural progression of each of these disease processes will be discussed. Provide a sound scientific foundation with which to approach evidence-based diagnosis, triage, and treatment of patients with acute versus chronic anorectal disorders.

title: Survey: Theories of Drama
description: Selected major critical and theoretical sources, from Aristotle to the present day; the influences of theories upon playwriting and modes of theatrical production.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription: This course will take a comparative approach to some major "theories of the theatre  that have emerged during periods of intense dramatic activity in cultures ranging widely in time and space: ancient Greece and India, classical Japan, early modern and modern Europe, the modern Americas, and the postcolonial societies of contemporary Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean. Drama, theatre, and performance are among the earliest forms of representation theorized in both Western and non-Western cultural traditions, and the parameters of theory are defined with remarkable consistency by the distinctive qualities of theatre as an "imitative,  performative, and public art. Theatre's likeness to life raises metaphysical, aesthetic, and formal issues, while the aspect of live performance engages the practical details of presentation and reception. Our discussion will take this duality into account, connecting theatre theory with general principles of poetics as well as the material, sociopolitical, and institutional contexts of performance in a given time and place. The readings will be organized into sequential units, including "Foundational Poetics,  "Classicism and Neoclassicism,  "Realism and its Redactions,  "Political Theatre,  "The Avant-Garde,  and "Postcolonial Revisions.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule: The course considers key works in theories of drama, theatre, and performance from the ancient Freek period to the present. Each 75-minute class will typically focus on an individual theorist, so there will be a steady movement forward in both time and space in terms of coverage.

Further, emphasis will be placed on understanding the experiences of those most-affected by historical and continuing segregation.

Explore planning as a tool for problem solving, planning and social change, the multiple roles in which planners find themselves, useful skills and perspectives, and areas of planning practice. Addresses core values, sustainability, equity and social justice, professional skills, and the role of plans in relation to policies and programs.

title: Policy-Making Process
description: Examines the political, social, and economic contexts that shape and are shaped by policy making processes. Though the focus is on the US, international comparisons will be made, and students are encouraged to think about the American context through comparative and international perspectives. Familiarizes students with dominant theories and models of policymaking process and policy change, starting with the model of the policy cycle. Focuses in on key topics and issues in policy making, specifically, agenda setting, implementation, and the relationships between policymaking and democracy. Reflects on contemporary and emerging issues and dilemmas of the politics of policy making.

title: Animal Biology Laboratory
description: General concepts of animal biology at an introductory level emphasizing the evolutionary relationships between animals. Learn about general body plans and strategies used to accomplish the basic tasks of staying alive in major animal groups using preserved and live animals. Study the diversity within each group of animals by integrating the body plans with the lifestyle and ecology of animals. Dissections of earthworm, freshwater mussel, squid, sea star, and rat aid the study of these general principles.

title: Freshwater: Past, Present, and Future
description: Freshwater is one of our most valuable resources, and the basis for life itself. Explores contemporary threats and issues relating to freshwater ecosystems (lakes, rivers, wetlands) ranging from local to global. Covers a broad range of topics in freshwater sciences (invasive species, harmful algal blooms, overfishing, pathogens in drinking water) to provide a representative cross-section of the field. Material will tie directly to local and global societal issues. Integrates insights from biology with other disciplines (chemistry, geosciences, social sciences) to offer a deeper understanding of the threats to freshwater ecosystems, and how this affects human well-being.

title: Tiny Earth: Antibiotic Discovery Research
description: Learn basic methodology in scientific research and discovery, including laboratory techniques, quantitative reasoning, scientific communication, and collaboration. Gain hands-on laboratory experience working with microbes to test original hypotheses concerning the discovery of potential antibiotic compounds while addressing the world's antibiotic resistance crisis by contributing data to the global "Tiny Earth" network of researchers to advance potential drug development. Tiny Earth seeks to encourage students to pursue careers in science through real-world, applied research experiences and aims to address a worldwide health threat of the diminishing supply of effective antibiotics by "student-sourcing antibiotic discovery." Concurrent enrollment in ZOOLOGY/BOTANY/BIOLOGY 152 is required for permission to enroll.

title: Marine Ecology
description: An introduction to the physical and chemical properties of marine habitats, how these properties influence the distribution of species and ecosystems, how interactions between species and their environment influence the organisms living in these habitats, and how these interactions relate to the cycling of energy, nutrients, and organic matter through food webs and ecosystems. Cover several different marine ecosystem types and explore adaptations that organisms have developed for living in these environments. Explore current threats facing marine species and habitats along with conservation strategies and successes.

instructorProvidedContent.instructorDescription:
A general marine ecology course. The course will begin with an introduction to the physical and chemical properties of marine habitats and how these influence the distribution of species and ecosystems. We will cover how interactions between species and their environment influence the organisms living in these habitats as well as how these relate to the cycling of energy, nutrients, and organic matter through food webs and ecosystems. We will dive into several different marine ecosystem types and explore adaptations that organisms have developed for living in these environments. Finally, we will explore current threats facing marine species and habitats along with conservation strategies and successes.
This is a lecture-based course that will also include in-class discussion activities.
instructorProvidedContent.typicalTopicsAndOrSchedule:
Part 1: Ocean habitats (structure and distribution, physical and chemical properties)
Part 2: Nutrients and primary production 
Part 3: Species interactions (herbivory, predation, competition, disease)
Part 4: Ecosystems (benthic, deep sea)
Part 5: Adaptation and movement
Part 6: Disturbance and conservation (climate change, pollution, fisheries, management)
instructorProvidedContent.format: In-person instruction 2x per week

title: Medical Entomology: Biology of Vector and Vector-borne Diseases
description: Explore the biological and molecular adaptations of parasitic arthropods that allow them to feed on vertebrate host and facilitate the transmission of vector-borne pathogens. Examines how anthropogenic activities, behaviors, and effects on climate affect the biology of vectors, the pathogens they transmit, and the emergence of vector-borne epidemics in the world. Emphasis on the molecular and physiological interaction between pathogens, their vector, and the vertebrate host and the fundamentals on how vectors and vector-borne pathogens cause disease in humans. Evaluate real control programs deployed globally for the control of vector-borne diseases.
